legacy.text:
The question of who held authority in the churches did not stay open forever. By around 200 CE, one bishop had become the common pattern almost everywhere, including in Rome. Rome had once been led by a council of elders. No text says how or when that change was actually felt. All that can be seen is that the older way quietly dropped out of the argument.

The texts of these churches did not survive evenly. Ignatius argued for the single bishop, and it took a two-century scholarly fight to settle which of his letters were genuine. Some scholars still doubt them. First Clement was copied into a great Bible manuscript. The Shepherd of Hermas was once read as scripture by three major later teachers, but it was later moved to the shelf newcomers were given to read. That was a real demotion, though not the outright ban later memory sometimes assumes. The Didache, a teaching manual from one of these communities, disappeared from use for roughly eighteen centuries. What survived best was not always what mattered most at the time. It may have been what a later settlement found useful to keep.

docstory-pahc.story.polycarp-forwards-le.text:
The Philippians asked for the letters of Ignatius, which the community at Smyrna had collected. Polycarp of Smyrna answered their request in a letter of his own to the church at Philippi.

The date of the letter is not certain, and it may be two letters joined into one. Polycarp opens it in his own name and that of the presbyters who are with him. He never calls himself bishop, though Ignatius writes to him as one, and Smyrna's letter on his death calls him its bishop.

He writes that he has sent the letters Ignatius wrote to Smyrna, along with all the others they had, just as the Philippians asked. The letters went with his own, and he told the Philippians they could gain a great deal from them.

story.text:
From about 70 to 200 CE, Christians gathered in households. They lived in Antioch and Syria, in the cities of western Asia Minor, and in Rome. Letters and travelers kept them joined as one, even as the last of the apostles' generation was passing and no central body ruled these churches.

These churches held that legitimate teaching and practice must trace back to what the apostles had testified. Rome's letter to Corinth sets out a chain: God sent Christ, Christ sent the apostles, and the apostles appointed successors. Ignatius, a bishop of Antioch, writes to several churches. He tells them to be subject to the bishop, as the apostles were subject to Christ.

The surviving letters give two different answers to who should lead once the apostles were gone. Ignatius's letters put one bishop at the center, with elders and deacons beside him, and one letter says the elders fit the bishop as strings fit a harp. In Rome, the surviving letters show a council of elders leading together. Ignatius addresses Polycarp, a church leader at Smyrna, as a bishop, yet Polycarp's own letter names him only beside the elders with him.

Letters held these scattered households together. The church at Rome wrote at length to Corinth, which had removed some of its elders from office. Rome argued that men who had served blamelessly should not have been removed. Seven surviving letters under Ignatius's name say he wrote them on a guarded journey toward Rome. Later, Polycarp sent the Philippians the letters of Ignatius that his church held, because they had asked for them.

Giving thanks over bread and cup stood at the center of these gatherings, and its order changed from one household to the next. One community's manual, the Didache, gives thanks over the cup before the bread, and it tells no story of a supper or a betrayal. Ignatius says that only a thanksgiving the bishop leads, or entrusts to another, counts as proper. Justin, a philosopher in Rome, describes a fuller Sunday gathering there.

The danger from the state was always there, but the actual incidents came and went. Tacitus, a Roman historian, reports that Nero blamed the Great Fire of Rome in 64 on a group the crowd called Christians. A great number, he says, were convicted and put to death. No source names one of them. About fifty years later, Pliny, the governor of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan for guidance. He found, in his words, "nothing but a depraved superstition that went too far." Trajan replied that Christians were not to be sought out, though those accused and convicted were to be punished.

Some communities read a death for the name as the completion of a life. Ignatius writes that he wants to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that he may be found the pure bread of Christ. The church at Smyrna told how Polycarp died. Its letter says the community kept his bones in a fitting place, where they hoped to gather each year, as they were able, to keep the day of his death. The same letter names Quintus, who came forward for trial and lost his nerve at the sight of the beasts. It says the gospel does not teach people to give themselves up. Only these two inside accounts survive, Ignatius's letters and Smyrna's letter, and both come from Antioch and Asia Minor.

By about 200, one bishop was becoming the dominant pattern, even in Rome. One modern scholar, Peter Lampe, thinks Rome may not have had a single bishop before Victor, its bishop from 189 to 199. The texts of these churches do not say how or when Rome changed. From about 180, writers in other regions argued from an apostolic line they treated as already secure.

docstory-pahc.story.nero-scapegoating.text:
In 64 a great fire burned through Rome. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some fifty years later, says a rumor spread that the fire had been set on orders. To get rid of that rumor, Nero shifted the blame onto a group the crowd called Christians.

Tacitus wrote from outside the Christian communities, and he had his own reasons for portraying Nero as monstrous. What he describes is one episode under one emperor. It is not certain that Christians, as a group known by that name, were punished after the fire. A more general memory from later years may have been attached to it.

Tacitus describes the Christians as hated for their vile acts. Those who confessed were arrested first, he reports, and on their information a great number were convicted. In his reading, they were condemned less for arson than for hatred of humankind.

No source names a single Christian who died in these events. Tacitus says they were put to death with cruelty meant as a show. Some were wrapped in the skins of beasts and torn apart by dogs, and others were fastened to crosses or set alight as torches after dark.

docstory-pahc.story.didache-eucharist.text:
A community that followed the Didache gave thanks over the cup first. "We thank you, our Father, for the holy vine of David your servant," the prayer begins. This picture is pieced together from the Didache's own instructions.

Then came thanks over the broken bread, for the life and knowledge made known through Jesus. The prayer says this bread was once scattered over the hills and was gathered together to become one. In the same way, it asks God to gather the Church from the ends of the earth into his kingdom. Nowhere in these prayers does anyone tell the story of a supper or a betrayal.

Only the baptized could eat or drink of this thanksgiving. After all had eaten their fill, a longer thanksgiving followed, for God's holy name and for knowledge and faith and immortality. It closed with the community's own cry, Maran atha, and then Amen.

Every Lord's day the community gathered to break bread and give thanks, after first confessing their sins. Anyone at odds with another had to be reconciled before joining in.

docstory-pahc.story.grandsons-before-dom.text:
This story comes from Hegesippus, a Christian of Palestine who wrote it down perhaps eighty years after it happened. It survives only because the bishop Eusebius quoted him long afterward.

Some of Jesus' own family were still alive. They were grandsons of Judas, who was called his brother, and they were reported to the emperor Domitian as being of the line of David. That mattered to Domitian, because he dreaded the coming of Christ as Herod had, so they were brought before him and questioned.

Were they of David's family? They said they were. Asked what they owned, they said they had only nine thousand denarii between them, and not in coin. That was the value of a piece of land of only thirty-nine acres. They still paid the dues on it, and they lived by working it themselves.

Then they held out their hands to show him the rough skin and the corns raised by constant labor. He asked them about Christ's kingdom and when it would come. They told him it was not of this world or of the earth, but belonged to heaven and the angels. It would appear at the end of time.

Domitian passed no sentence. He treated them with contempt, as beneath his notice, and he let them go and called off the persecution. Once they were released, they became leaders of the churches.

docstory-pahc.story.first-clement-corint.text:
The church at Corinth had removed some of its presbyters, its elders, from office, and the church at Rome answered with a long letter. The letter names no author, though later tradition says Clement wrote it. It is usually dated around 96, though it may be as late as 140.

Rome's letter says the presbyters had served blamelessly and with honor. Only Rome's letter survives, so Corinth's own side of the dispute is lost.

The letter takes up the removal directly. It gives example after example of jealousy and strife destroying what unity had built. Rome wrote as one church to another, out of concern, and it could only appeal. It gave no orders the way a later church authority would.

Corinth's action, the letter argues, broke proper order, and it calls on those who started the revolt to submit to the presbyters.

docstory-pahc.story.ignatius-guarded-jou.text:
In the letters that carry his name, Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, says that he was condemned and sent under armed guard on the long road to Rome. There he expected to be thrown to the beasts in the arena. It is not certain that he wrote the letters himself. They may have been written later, in Rome, under his name.

He says he was bound to ten leopards, by which he means his band of soldiers. They only grew worse, he says, when they were treated kindly. Churches came out to meet him along the way, and at Smyrna he was met by delegations from Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles.

On the road he wrote at least seven letters that survive. He urged each community to gather around one bishop and one eucharist, and he pressed the point hard, which suggests that unity was still being argued over.

He asked Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, to write for him to the nearby churches. He thanked the church at Smyrna for welcoming his companions and for not being ashamed of his chains. He sent a letter ahead to the church at Rome, asking them not to step in to save his life. He called himself the wheat of God. He asked to be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, so that he might be found the pure bread of Christ.

docstory-pahc.story.pliny-interrogation.text:
Pliny the Younger was the Roman governor of Bithynia and Pontus. Writing to the emperor Trajan, he says he was unsure how to handle accusations against Christians, so he asked the emperor. He had already questioned those accused, and he executed those who held to the name after repeated warnings.

Some of the accused told him they had once been Christians but had given it up. They said they used to meet on a fixed day before dawn and sing a song in turns to Christ as God. They had bound themselves by an oath to commit no theft, robbery or adultery, and never to break faith or refuse to return a deposit. Then they parted, and later met again to share a meal of ordinary food, which they said was harmless. What that meal was, no one can say for certain.

To learn the truth, he tortured two enslaved women who were called ministrae. The word may be a title, deaconesses, though that reading is disputed. The women left no words of their own, and all that survives is what Pliny chose to record. What he found, in his own words, was "nothing but a depraved superstition that went too far."

Trajan's reply survives, and it says Pliny had acted rightly. Christians were not to be hunted out. Those accused and convicted were to be punished, and anyone who denied the name and proved it by act was to be pardoned. Anonymous accusations were to be refused as a very bad precedent.

docstory-pahc.story.justin-sunday-gather.text:
Justin wrote to the emperor and the Roman Senate to defend Christian practice. He tells them plainly what his community at Rome does on the day named for the sun. He does not say whether the churches of Antioch or Asia Minor followed the same order.

On that day, those who live in the cities and in the countryside gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read for as long as time permits. Then the one presiding gives a talk, urging the people to imitate these good things, and all rise together and pray.

Bread and wine and water are brought. The one presiding offers prayers and thanksgivings according to his ability, and the people give their assent by saying Amen. Those who have means and are willing give what they choose, and the gifts are left with him.

The one presiding cares for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison and strangers passing through. In a word, Justin writes, he looks after everyone who is in need.

docstory-pahc.story.quintus-recantation.text:
Before Polycarp's own flight and arrest, the letter from Smyrna that honors his death tells of another man.

Quintus was a Phrygian who had lately come from Phrygia. He forced himself and some others to come forward for trial of their own accord, but when he actually saw the wild beasts, he lost his nerve. After much urging, the proconsul persuaded him to swear the oath and offer sacrifice.

The letter says plainly that the church does not praise those who give themselves up, because the Gospel does not teach people to do so. Polycarp did the opposite. When he first heard that he was being sought, he was not troubled at all. He meant to stay in the city, but at the wish of many he agreed to leave.

He went to a country house not far from the city and stayed there with a few companions, praying night and day. When his pursuers came near, he moved to another house. He did not go looking for arrest. He was found only after two young men of his household were seized, and one of them, under torture, told his pursuers where he was.

docstory-pahc.story.martyrdom-of-polycar.text:
This is how the church at Smyrna remembered Polycarp, its aged bishop, in a letter to the church at Philomelium. It is told in the style these churches used to honor their martyrs, and no outside account survives to check it.

His community urged Polycarp to hide, and he withdrew for a time, until someone in his own household gave him away under torture. Before the proconsul he was pressed to swear by Caesar's fortune and curse Christ, and then he would be spared. Polycarp answered that he had served Christ for eighty-six years and Christ had never done him any wrong. How then, he asked, could he blaspheme his King and his Savior?

The crowd first cried out for a lion, but the official in charge said it was not lawful, because the wild-beast shows were already over. So they cried out that he should be burned alive. When the fire was lit, the account says, it formed an arch around him, like the sail of a ship filled by the wind. An executioner was sent to finish him with a dagger, and the account says so much blood came out that it put out the fire.

Afterward the community gathered his bones, which they held more precious than the finest jewels, and laid them in a fitting place. There they hoped to gather each year, as they were able, to keep the day of his martyrdom. They would remember those who had finished the course and prepare those still to walk it.

story.text:
From about 150 to 400 CE, Christians in Alexandria and across Egypt passed on one faith in two ways. Through long study together, teachers formed the few who could read, while baptism, the Eucharist and the yearly round of fasts and feasts reached everyone else.

Both ways answered to one center, the Logos. He is God's Word, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. Through him, Scripture, learning, worship and the remaking of a person became one movement toward one God.

Origen taught that Scripture, like a person, has body, soul and spirit: a plain sense, and deeper senses that point to Christ and the soul. This way of reading is called allegoria. But the bishop Nepos wrote a book against it, and village churches in the Arsinoite district followed his book. After Nepos died, Bishop Dionysius answered them with three days of open argument, and the leader of the other side was persuaded.

Alexandria had a long tradition of Christian teachers and their pupils. The first name kept is Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher who became a Christian. Clement taught in the city from about 180. He praised his last teacher as the true bee, who gathered from the flowers of the prophets and apostles and left a deathless knowledge in his hearers' souls. Clement gives no name, and Eusebius says it was Pantaenus. Origen came after Clement, and Eusebius says he led the teaching of those preparing for baptism from his eighteenth year. Scholars disagree on whether a formal school stood behind these names before Origen's time.

A teacher and a bishop each held real authority, and the two never became one. The teacher's standing came from the wisdom people saw in him, while the bishop held an office handed down. In the early 230s, Eusebius reports, bishops in Palestine ordained Origen, the city's greatest teacher. His own bishop, Demetrius, had not agreed, and he condemned the ordination and the teacher with it. Origen left for Caesarea and never taught in the city again.

Persecution came more than once. Origen's father was beheaded about 202, and Origen himself was jailed and tortured under Decius. The church held two pictures of a life fully formed: the martyr's witness unto death, and the soul's long climb toward God. About 260, plague struck Alexandria. Bishop Dionysius wrote that most of his people did not run. They nursed the sick, and many caught the sickness and died.

Then the danger came from inside, as brothers argued over the very confession of the Word. Arius taught that the Son was the highest creature and not fully God. In 325 the council at Nicaea answered with the word homoousios, meaning of one substance with the Father. Athanasius, bishop from 328 to 373, defended it through five exiles. Later he wrote that the bishops had added nothing new, and that they had fenced what the churches had received. He also wrote that the Word became human so that people could share God's own life.

After Nicaea, the bishop of Alexandria became the guard of the creed across Egypt. His tools were letters, councils and exile. Among those who could read, the long bond between teacher and student was no longer the main way faith was formed.

Later tradition ends the line of teachers with Didymus and says he headed the school in its last years. Didymus was blind from the age of four, too young to have learned letters, and he died about 398, at eighty-five.

The Nicene creed and the hope of sharing God's life reached Eastern Christianity, and so did the habit of reading Scripture with Christ at its center. Origen's work was carried forward too, and people loved it and argued over it.

legacy.text:
Two things from the Christians of Alexandria lived on past their own time, in different ways. The first was a settled inheritance. The church there passed on the Nicene confession, the hope of sharing God's own life, and Scripture read for a deeper meaning beneath its surface. Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus, teachers of a later generation, gathered an anthology of Origen's own writing before that age had ended.

The second thing was a live argument, not a settled one. Origen's boldest ideas kept being read, loved and contested by turns, and translators who had taken a side carried them forward, on both sides of the argument. The argument finally broke into open controversy right around the year 400.

docstory-alx.story.john-young-robber.text:
In a city not far from Ephesus, the aged apostle John once left a promising young man in the bishop's care. Clement, a teacher in Alexandria, passed this on as a true account, handed down and kept in memory.

The bishop taught the young man and baptized him. Then he relaxed his watch, and the young man fell in with idle companions, and then with worse ones. At last he ran to the hills and became chief of a band of robbers.

Years later John came back and asked the bishop to return what he had left in his keeping. The bishop wept and said the young man was dead to God, a robber on the mountain. The old apostle tore his clothes, called for a horse and rode out to the mountain himself.

When the young man saw him, he fled, but John forgot his age and rode after him. He begged his child not to run from his own father, old and unarmed. There was still hope of life for him, John said, and he would answer for him to Christ.

The young man stopped, threw down his weapons and wept. John led him back, prayed with him and fasted beside him in the struggle, and he did not leave until he had restored him to the church.

docstory-alx.story.leonides-martyrdom.text:
About the year 202, under the emperor Severus, persecution struck Alexandria. Leonides was arrested and held for beheading, and his son Origen was sixteen. Eusebius tells what happened next in that house. He wrote a century later, from the Alexandrian church's memory, from Origen's own letters and from reports about him.

The boy burned to give himself up and die beside his father. His mother begged him to spare her, but he would not listen. So she hid all his clothes, and shame kept him at home.

Origen did the one thing left to him: he wrote to his father in prison. One line of that letter survives, "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."

Leonides did not change his mind. He was beheaded, and the family's property was seized. Origen, not yet seventeen, was left the eldest of seven children, with a widowed mother.

docstory-alx.story.potamiaena.text:
When Eusebius wrote, Potamiaena was still famous among the people of the country for all she had endured. Her story reached him already shaped by devotion.

She was a young woman put to death under the emperor Severus, and her mother Marcella died with her. She was threatened with rape, the cruelty the age kept for women, but she stood fast. The tradition says the judge sentenced her to die by burning pitch, poured slowly.

A soldier named Basilides led her out. The tradition says he held back the crowd's abuse with such gentleness that she told him to take courage. She promised, it says, to ask her Lord for him when she was gone.

Not long after, his fellow soldiers asked Basilides to swear an oath. He refused, because he was a Christian. At first they thought he was joking, but he was not, and he was put in prison. The tradition says that when fellow Christians came to ask him why, he told them: Potamiaena had come to him in the night and set a crown on his head.

The church baptized him in prison, and then he was beheaded.

docstory-alx.story.origen-daring-deed.text:
Origen was still young and teaching the faith in Alexandria, where he taught men and women together, day and night.

Eusebius alone tells what Origen did then, and no account from Origen himself describes it. Eusebius says Origen took a hard verse from Matthew in the most literal sense. It speaks of those who "have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake." By this account he acted on it himself, both to fulfill Christ's word and so that no one could accuse him of wrong, since he taught women as well as men. He tried to keep it secret, but he could not. Eusebius calls the act immature, and in the same breath a proof of unusual faith.

When his bishop, Demetrius, learned of it, he admired the young man's daring and faith and urged him to keep teaching. Later, once Origen had grown famous beyond Alexandria, the same Demetrius turned that youthful act against him. He wrote to bishops everywhere calling it foolish, and he also attacked Origen's ordination by the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem.

Some have doubted that it happened at all, and thought the report grew from Origen's own figures of speech. Others see no reason to doubt it.

Origen himself later judged the verse differently. He wrote against reading it so literally.

docstory-alx.story.origen-demetrius.text:
For years the teacher and the bishop held together. Demetrius governed the church of Alexandria and Origen taught, and the fame of the school filled the city.

Nearly everything known of what came next comes from Eusebius, who admired Origen and was hostile to the memory of Demetrius.

The break came over authority. On a journey through Palestine, Origen was ordained a presbyter by the bishops there, though his own bishop had not agreed to it. Demetrius condemned the ordination, and the teacher with it.

Around his forty-sixth year, Origen left Alexandria for Caesarea, and he never taught in the city again.

The church kept both memories, the office that had to be honored and the teacher. What each man said, and with what heart, cannot now be heard. The synods' rulings from the break are lost.

docstory-alx.story.gregory-formation.text:
Origen did not begin with doctrines, Gregory says. He began like a farmer testing soil: he questioned young Gregory and dug into his mind to see what it did under pressure.

Gregory had come from Neo-Caesarea, in Pontus, to study law. At Caesarea he met Origen and stayed some five years. He tells how he was taught in a farewell speech of praise, though it is not settled whether Gregory gave that speech, or when.

Logic came first, to make thinking honest. Next came the natural world, geometry and the stars, until the students' sense of wonder was trained. Then came ethics, formed as habits, with the teacher's own life teaching as well. Only after that came theology, where they read everything the philosophers and poets had said of God, with Scripture at the center.

Under all of it, Gregory says, something else was happening. Love was kindled in his inmost soul, like a spark falling there: love for the holy Word, and for this man who was the Word's friend. Gregory gave up the law, and when at last he had to leave, he called it being driven out of paradise.

docstory-alx.story.arsinoite-conference.text:
The village churches near Arsinoe loved a bishop named Nepos, who had written a book against the allegorists. The promises in Scripture, he said, meant a thousand-year kingdom of plenty on this earth, plainly read. Nepos had died, and his book now ruled whole congregations. That book is lost, and it is known only from the bishop who answered it.

Bishop Dionysius went out to the villages. He told the story himself in his book On the Promises, which Eusebius later quoted. He called together the elders and the teachers, and any of the people who wished to come. For three days, from morning to evening, he sat with them and examined the book, argument by argument.

Afterward he wrote that he loved Nepos for his faith, his hard work in the Scriptures and his psalms. Even so, he wrote, "the truth must be loved and honored most of all." He rejoiced in the constancy and sincerity of the believers, and in their willingness to reconsider as they weighed the arguments together.

At the end, Coracion, the leader of the other side, was persuaded, and he said so in front of everyone. Some of the other believers, the account says, were glad at the spirit of agreement all had shown.

docstory-alx.story.plague-nursing.text:
A great sickness came to Alexandria about the year 260, and every house had its dead. Bishop Dionysius wrote to the churches at festival time, while the plague still raged.

Most of the brothers and sisters did not run, he wrote. They visited the sick without fear, tended them day after day and served them in Christ.

Many caught the sickness from those they nursed, and they died of it. He wrote that they died most joyfully, as if drawing their neighbors' pain onto themselves. He wrote that they took the bodies of the dead in their open hands, washed and dressed them, and carried them away.

In the same letter, he said the pagans thrust away their own sick at the first sign of illness, and fled even from their dearest.

docstory-alx.story.didymus-meeting.text:
Didymus lost his sight at four, he told Palladius, too young ever to have learned to read. Palladius met him four times over ten years and wrote down what he saw.

By then Didymus was old. What others took in with their eyes, he had taken in through his ears and held on to, and he interpreted Scripture word by word. Palladius calls him the blind author. Jerome, who studied with him briefly, wrote in 392 or 393 that Didymus had already passed his eighty-third year.

Later tradition called him the seer, a name set against his blindness. Most of the books he wrote are lost, and only fragments were recovered, centuries later.

He died at the age of eighty-five.

story.text:
From about 325 to 394, churches in Cappadocia and Pontus held to the faith of the Council of Nicaea. Nearly everything that survives from them was written by three men. Two were brothers, Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa. The third, Gregory of Nazianzus, had been Basil's friend since their student days.

These churches held that the Son is fully what the Father is, and that the Holy Spirit is no lesser presence trailing behind them. Two Greek words carried the idea. Ousia meant what God is, one being, and hypostasis meant who God is. Father, Son and Holy Spirit were each a real someone, none a costume and none a creature. Their word for reverence, eusebeia, covered exact words about God, and it also covered right living, with money and power included.

About 368, drought struck Caesarea and its countryside. Landowners with full storehouses held back their grain and waited for higher prices. Basil, then a priest, preached against them. He charged that to hoard a neighbor's bread while the neighbor starves is theft, whatever the law calls it. Granaries opened, and relief was organized for as long as the crisis lasted.

Basil became bishop of Caesarea in 370. Later he built a poorhouse outside the city walls, with a guest-house, an infirmary and a house for people with leprosy, where ascetics served as nurses. Gregory of Nazianzus called it the new city.

For most of this period the court backed a rival creed, which held the Son to be merely like the Father. In 371 or 372 the emperor Valens sent his prefect Modestus to bring Basil into line. According to Gregory, Basil's friend, Modestus threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death. Basil is remembered answering that a man who owns nothing has nothing to confiscate.

One flashpoint in the fight over the Holy Spirit was a prayer. About 375, Basil prayed with his people and gave glory to the Father in two forms: with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, and through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Basil reports that some who heard him called his words new and contradictory. To glorify the Spirit together with the Father and the Son placed the Spirit on the Creator's side of the line.

Amphilochius of Iconium, a younger bishop and friend, asked Basil to answer in writing, and the answer became a book, On the Holy Spirit. Basil argued that the words of worship carry what the church believes. Yet in his own writings he never plainly called the Spirit God. His allies argued about this at the time, with some wanting the plain word and others defending his restraint.

Macrina was the family's eldest child, and her circle called her the Teacher. She led a community of ascetic women on the family estate at Annisa. In 379 her brother Gregory of Nyssa found her dying. He later shaped their last talk into a dialogue on the soul and the resurrection, and scholars disagree on how much of it is hers.

Gregory of Nazianzus carried the argument to Constantinople. In 379 he came to lead the small Nicene church there, but a rival church, long favored by the court, still held the city's great churches. So his people met in a private house he named Anastasia, which means resurrection, and there he preached the five Theological Orations.

The tide turned under a new emperor, Theodosius, who favored the Nicene faith. In 381 the Council of Constantinople met. Gregory of Nazianzus was made bishop of the city and given the council's presiding chair, but he did not hold it long. He resigned before the work was done. By his own telling, his election was disputed and he was worn out.

The council ratified the faith of Nicaea. Its creed says the Holy Spirit is worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. The bishops wrote the faith the way these churches had already been singing it. Eastern Orthodox churches still confess this creed, and Roman Catholics honor Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus as teachers of the whole church.

legacy.text:
The teachers of these churches did not stay local. Their names and arguments became curriculum, liturgy and law for later traditions. Those traditions trace their roots through the councils these churches lived through and helped write. Orthodox, Catholic and, more distantly, Protestant teaching all still argue in vocabulary this circle fought to place.

One thing, though, is not so simple. Did the three teachers ever share one settled scheme, or did they pursue three related projects that later tradition flattened into one tidy story? Historians now dispute this. Even the letter most often cited to prove their agreement is in doubt, since many scholars now think it was written not by Basil but by his brother Gregory.

docstory-cappadocian.story.forty-sebaste.text:
It was around the year 320, in one of the last persecutions. At Sebaste in Lesser Armenia, forty soldiers were condemned for being Christians.

As the churches of Basil's day remembered it, they were stripped and made to stand through a winter night on a frozen pond. A warm bath steamed on the shore, offered to any man who would deny the faith and step out of the cold.

The tradition says one of the forty broke before the night ended and went to the warm water. It says a guard set to watch them was moved by what he saw. He took off his own clothes and joined the rest on the ice, confessing the faith the other man had just abandoned, so the martyrs still numbered forty. All of them died.

Basil and Gregory of Nyssa both preached on the feast of the Forty. Their mother, Emmelia, is remembered for building the family's chapel at Annisa for the Forty, where the relics were placed.

docstory-cappadocian.story.athens-friend.text:
Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus met as students, most likely at Athens. Both had gone there for the fullest education their world offered.

Gregory's memory of Athens comes from the great funeral speech he gave for Basil, years afterward. He wrote it after the friendship had met real trouble, the wound of Sasima among it, and that trouble had not been simply resolved before Basil died. Yet when Gregory rose to praise his dead friend, he chose to remember Athens first.

What grew between them, Gregory said, was one soul lodged in two bodies. They were housemates, messmates and close friends. Worldly advancement was not their aim, he says. The sole business of both was virtue, the fullest possible turn toward God.

Of Basil's earlier schooling, Gregory used the image of the busy bee, which gathers what is most useful from every flower.

When their studies ended, both men went home to Cappadocia.

docstory-cappadocian.story.julian-school.text:
Julian spent part of his boyhood at Macellum, an estate in Cappadocia. His family had been purged, and he was kept there under Christian tutors he did not choose. As a grown man he rejected that schooling entirely and turned back to the old gods and to the classical culture.

Julian ruled as emperor from 361 to 363. He issued a school law, and separately a second, narrower ruling aimed at Christian teachers. Those who taught Homer and the old poets, he ruled, must believe in the gods those texts honored, or stop teaching them. His reasoning survives in his own words. A Christian teacher who explained stories he said he did not believe was dishonest, Julian argued, at the very root of his craft.

The measure struck at the Greek learning, the paideia, which the leaders of these churches had spent their lives mastering and had defended as compatible with their faith. Julian is also remembered for taking measures against Caesarea itself, in the region of his own schooling, because of its Christian loyalties.

Julian died on campaign in Persia in 363, but the fury of Gregory of Nazianzus outlived him. Gregory wrote a pair of speeches against the dead emperor, ferocious even for attacks of that kind. They refused Julian any of the honor a dead emperor might expect.

docstory-cappadocian.story.famine-open-b.text:
The harvest failed. Drought had struck Caesarea and the country around it in the years before Basil became bishop, and grain grew scarce and dear. Those with full storehouses held their grain back, waiting for the price to climb higher before they would sell.

Basil, a priest then, preached against them and did not soften the charge. To hoard a neighbor's bread while that neighbor starves is theft, he taught, whatever the law calls it. He pointed to the man in the Gospel parable who tore down his barns to build bigger ones, a man who learned the lesson too late.

Basil preached against lending at interest for the same reason: to profit from another person's desperate need was the same kind of wrong.

Then the granaries opened. Relief was organized for the hungry, paid for and handed out for as long as the crisis lasted.

docstory-cappadocian.story.valens-caesar.text:
As Gregory of Nazianzus told it in his funeral speech for Basil, Modestus threatened the bishop with confiscation, exile, torture and death. Modestus was the praetorian prefect of the emperor Valens, and the emperor had sent him to bring Basil of Caesarea into line.

This was in 371 and 372. Valens backed a different creed from Basil's, and in those same years he split Cappadocia into two provinces, with real consequences for the churches. The prefect came ahead of the emperor's own visit.

Basil replied, the story goes, that a man who owns nothing has nothing to confiscate. No place is exile, he said, to one who counts the whole earth as God's. A man already given over to God in this life has nothing left that death can take.

The prefect, astonished, is said to have reported that no one had ever spoken to him that way. Basil is remembered replying that perhaps the prefect had never yet met a bishop.

The next Epiphany, Valens came to Caesarea himself. Gregory says he found the church crowded to its doors for the feast. The singing filled the whole building like the sea, and Basil presided in full order, unafraid. The emperor was shaken by what he saw, Gregory says.

According to Gregory, a decree of exile was later signed. It was never carried out, he says, because the emperor's son fell ill. Basil was not removed.

docstory-cappadocian.story.sasima-wound.text:
Sasima was a small posting, a dusty village where the mail changed horses.

In 372 Cappadocia was divided into two provinces, and a rival bishop claimed authority over the new province's land. Basil moved to secure his authority as metropolitan, the chief bishop of the province. He created new sees and consecrated allies to hold them. Sasima was one, and Basil named his close friend, Gregory of Nazianzus, to it.

Gregory felt the appointment as a wound. His bitter letters and poems tell it, and so does the long poem about his life that he wrote years later. No record from Basil's side survives.

Gregory had been pressed into an office he had not sought, in a miserable little village. As Gregory understood it, he was sent there more for Basil's need in the fight than for Gregory's own good.

Gregory in effect refused the post, and he probably never governed it. His aging father, then bishop of Nazianzus, begged him to stay and help.

docstory-cappadocian.story.doxology-stan.text:
Basil, bishop of Caesarea, prayed with his people in years when the imperial court still pressed its creed on the churches. He gave glory in two forms. One was to the Father with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit. The other was to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.

Some who heard it objected. His words were new, they said, and contradicted each other. The difference lay in a few small words, but everyone understood that it mattered. To glorify the Spirit together with the Father and the Son places the Spirit on the Creator's side of the line.

His younger friend Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, asked Basil to set the whole argument down, and the answer became a book. Basil examined the church's giving of glory word by word. Not everything the church holds came to it in writing, he argued, and the prayer under attack had come down to the church in that unwritten way.

Pressed to declare in one bare sentence that the Spirit is God, Basil measured his words. He said it in the church's own way, through worship, through the Spirit's rank, and through the Name spoken over the baptized. Some of his own allies wanted the plain word spoken, while other friends defended his restraint.

Years later, when the bishops gathered again, they wrote the faith the way these churches had already been singing it. Their creed says the Spirit is worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

docstory-cappadocian.story.nyssa-exile.text:
Under the emperor Valens, Gregory of Nyssa was deposed and driven into exile. He was still a fairly junior bishop, and his see was a minor one. He was charged with mishandling money.

His brother Basil wrote about the affair in letters defending him. In Basil's telling, the charges were trumped up. Hostile bishops of the court's party, who held the Son merely like the Father, had arranged them, he wrote. They used a synod packed against his brother, with no true hearing of the case.

Gregory spent about two years away from his see. He came back only when the political weather changed and Valens eased his pressure on the Nicene bishops of the region. A short note by Gregory himself survives, and it records something of his joy at coming back.

docstory-cappadocian.story.macrina-death.text:
In 379, Gregory of Nyssa traveled to see his sister Macrina. She was the eldest of the family's children, and her circle called her simply the Teacher. He found her already dying.

She lay on a plank set on the ground instead of a couch, wrapped in a rough garment, with no possessions around her.

As she was dying, brother and sister talked about the soul, about the resurrection, and about whether death should be feared. Everything that survives of this comes through Gregory's own pen. He wrote a Life of Macrina soon after, and he also shaped their last talk into a full dialogue, On the Soul and Resurrection. He staged it at her deathbed, in the manner of Plato's account of the last hours of Socrates. It is not known how much of her part is her own and how much is his.

Macrina died that evening. Gregory says plainly that he wept, and that he struggled through the funeral rites. A crowd gathered for her burial at the family chapel at Annisa, where earlier generations already lay. Gregory says the company of virgins she had gathered and led came with the crowd.

docstory-cappadocian.story.gregory-const.text:
The house was called Anastasia, which means resurrection. Gregory of Nazianzus gave it that name when he came to Constantinople in 379 to lead the small Nicene flock there. They worshipped in that private house because a rival party, long favored by the emperors, still held the city's great churches.

There Gregory preached five sermons, later called the Theological Orations. In them he defended the doctrine of the Trinity to a capital he found mostly hostile to it, or uncaring.

Then the tide turned, and a new emperor, Theodosius, favored the Nicene faith. A council met that would become the Council of Constantinople of 381. Gregory was made bishop of the city and given the council's presiding chair.

He did not hold the chair long. By his own account, some disputed whether his election was lawful under church rules, and he was also worn out by the whole contest. He resigned before the council's work was done and gave a farewell oration on his way out.

story.text:
Between about 320 and 430, Christians in Egypt left their villages for the edge of the desert. The last empire-wide persecution had ended between 311 and 313, and until then, dying for the faith had been a way to offer everything. The monks spoke of their own struggle as total combat, against demons and the tempting thoughts they stirred in a person's mind. Athanasius links that struggle to martyrdom once, for Antony alone. That it took martyrdom's place for the whole movement is a later reading, not something the sources say outright. These Christians saw the leaving itself as the whole work of a Christian life.

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote the Life of Antony between about 356 and 362, and the movement's founding portrait rests mostly on that one book. Scholars question how far its details are history. Athanasius says Antony was about eighteen or twenty when his parents died. That was about 270. Soon after, Antony heard the Gospel read in church as if it had been read for him, gave the family land to the villagers, and then gave away the rest.

Antony then left in stages. He lived first near his village, then in an abandoned fort across the river, and last on a mountain in the inner desert, three days' journey out. Athanasius gives a reason only for the last move: crowds kept finding Antony, and he wanted quiet. By this account he stayed on that mountain for most of the rest of his life.

Not every monk lived alone. About 320, Pachomius gathered monks into a community at Tabennesi. Palladius, a monk who lived in Egypt, wrote long after Pachomius died, and he says an angel gave Pachomius a tablet with a rule on it. Tradition says the community had nine houses for men and two for women when he died in 346, and it puts the members, roughly, in the low thousands.

Monks also lived in settlements such as Nitria, Kellia and Scete, where they kept small cells and gathered once a week for worship. Authority worked in two ways. Hermits and the monks of the settlements looked to an elder called abba or amma, a person whose wisdom had been proved. Elders held no office. In Pachomius's houses, by contrast, a written rule and appointed offices governed. Even so, people remembered Pachomius himself as a father-elder. Both kinds of authority stood side by side through these years.

The desert had no fixed course of study, and discernment did that work. Called diakrisis, it was the skill of judging how much discipline a particular person could bear. In the collected sayings of the elders, one pattern recurs: an eager newcomer asks an elder for an extreme practice, and the elder steers him toward something more moderate.

Evagrius was a formally educated man. Basil of Caesarea ordained him a reader, and Gregory of Nazianzus made him a deacon. About 385 he settled at Kellia, where he lived for fourteen years. There he wrote a system for the struggle. It sorted the tempting thoughts, the logismoi, into eight kinds, and it set out a path from practice to freedom from passion, and then to contemplation. The system belonged to him and his learned circle.

Evagrius died at Kellia in January 399. That year Theophilus, the bishop of Alexandria, sent an Easter letter saying that God has no human body. John Cassian, a monk who had lived at Scete, wrote about it decades later. He reports that almost all the monks of Egypt took the letter badly: they felt it went against Scripture, which they took to give God a human form. Theophilus then reversed course, for reasons scholars dispute, and campaigned against the followers of the teacher Origen.

In 400, a council at Alexandria condemned Origen and the monks who followed him. That year four monk leaders called the Tall Brothers, and others among them, had to leave Egypt, and the circle around Evagrius was broken up.

legacy.text:
The eight named kinds of tempting thought taught in the desert did not stay there. They passed west through Cassian's Conferences. Two centuries later Gregory the Great narrowed them, and they became the seven deadly sins of later Western moral teaching.

One popular link does not actually hold. The monks' word for the stillness they sought was hesychia. People often assume it names the same practice as the later Byzantine Hesychast tradition, with its Jesus Prayer technique. But that systematized method belongs to a separate, later tradition. It is not part of the desert monks' own record.

docstory-desert.story.antony-call.text:
Athanasius writes that Antony was about eighteen or twenty when his parents died, which left him with a little sister and the care of the house.

Less than six months later, as he went into church as he always did, he was thinking of how the apostles had left everything to follow the Savior. The Gospel was being read. He heard the Lord say to the rich man: "If you want to be perfect, go and sell what you have and give to the poor. Then come and follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven."

Antony went out of the church at once, as though the passage had been read on his account. He gave the villagers his family's land, three hundred Egyptian field measures of good ground. He sold everything else he could move and gave the money to the poor, keeping back a little for his sister.

Later he went into church again and heard the Lord say, "Do not be anxious about tomorrow." He could stay no longer. He went out and gave the rest to the poor as well, and he placed his sister with known and faithful virgins to be brought up. From then on he gave himself to a life of discipline outside his house, training himself with patience.

In the next village lived an old man who had been a hermit from his youth, and after Antony had seen him, he copied his devotion.

docstory-desert.story.antony-tomb-combat.text:
Athanasius writes that Antony went to the tombs, which lay some distance from the village. He asked an acquaintance to bring him bread at long intervals, then entered a tomb, and the man shut the door on him.

One night, he says, the enemy came with a crowd of demons and beat him until he lay speechless. Next day the acquaintance found him lying as though dead and carried him to the village church, where kinsfolk and villagers sat around him as around a corpse.

About midnight Antony came to himself. Everyone else was asleep, so he motioned to the acquaintance and asked to be carried back to the tombs.

Alone again, he lay unable to stand. That night the demons seemed to break through the walls in the likeness of lions, bears, leopards, serpents and wolves. Antony mocked them: "If you had any real power, it would have been enough for just one of you to come. But the Lord has made you weak. So you try to frighten me with your numbers."

Then the roof seemed to open, and a ray of light came down. The demons vanished and the pain stopped. Antony asked, "Where were you? Why did you not appear at the start, to end my pain?" A voice answered: "Antony, I was here, but I waited to see your fight. You have endured and have not given way. So I will always help you, and I will make your name known everywhere."

docstory-desert.story.antony-withdrawal.text:
Antony left the world in stages. First he lived near his own village, as all did who wished to train in those days, copying the devotion of an old hermit he had seen in the next village.

Later he found a fort on the far side of the river. It had stood empty so long that it was full of creeping things. Antony crossed over and lived there, and the creatures, Athanasius wrote, fled at once as if someone were chasing them. He built up the entrance completely and stored six months of loaves, and he found water inside. He stayed alone, never going out and never looking at anyone who came, and loaves were let down to him from above twice a year.

Friends who came were not let in. They often spent days and nights outside, and they heard what sounded like crowds clamoring within.

Nearly twenty years later he came out, and in time, Athanasius says, he was beset by many people and could not be still. Then a voice came to him from above and told him that, if he truly wanted quiet, he should go into the inner desert. He journeyed three days and three nights with Saracens, desert nomads, who were going that way. He came to a very lofty mountain, with a clear spring at its foot, a plain, and a few uncared-for palm trees. He recognized the place as his own home and stayed.

docstory-desert.story.pachomius-founding.text:
Palladius tells of a man named Pachomius, who lived at Tabennisi in the Thebaid and, he says, was counted worthy of prophecies and of angelic visions. Palladius says an angel appeared to him as he sat in his cave. The angel told him he had ordered his own life well, so it was pointless to stay in the cave any longer. He was to go out, gather all the young monks, and live with them.

The angel gave him a brass tablet with a rule written on it. Each man was to eat and drink according to his strength, and his work was to match that strength. Pachomius objected that the prayers it set were few, and the angel answered that he had given the rule so that even the little ones would keep it. The perfect, he said, need no rule, because alone in their cells they have given their whole lives to the contemplation of God.

In his own day, Palladius says, the monasteries that kept this rule held some seven thousand men. The first and great monastery was the one where Pachomius himself had lived, and he gives it thirteen hundred members.

docstory-desert.story.angel-hands-the-ta.text:
The Ethiopic rule of Pachomius begins by saying where it came from. Its first words are: "In the name of the holy Trinity. This is the rule which the angel of the Lord gave to Abba Pachomius as a command."

The text then tells a story. In a place called Tabennesis, in the province of Thebes, lived a man named Pachomius, one of those who led a clean life. Knowledge was given to him, and also the sight of angels. As he sat in his cave, the angel of the Lord appeared to him. The angel said that Pachomius had become perfect in his own life, and that living on in the cave was now needless. He should go out, gather the less perfect young men, and live with them, teaching them the rule as the angel gave it to him.

The angel then handed him a tablet of iron with the rule written on it. At the end of the rule's commands, Pachomius answered the angel: "These prayers are few." The angel said he had commanded it so that the weak also might keep the rule without grieving themselves. The perfect do not desire a rule for themselves. These things, he said, he had ordained for those who have no advisers.

docstory-desert.story.arsenius-flee.text:
The collected sayings tell of Abba Arsenius when he was in the palace. He prayed to God, "Lord, show me how to live." A voice came to him and said, "Arsenius, flee from men, and you will live."

A second saying tells of the time when he was living the ascetic life in the monastery. He prayed the same prayer, and again he heard a voice. It said, "Arsenius, flee. Keep silence. Live a life of silent contemplation. These are the basic causes that keep a person from sinning."

docstory-desert.story.moses-leaking-jug.text:
The sayings tell of a brother at Scete, the camp of the monks, who committed an offense. A congregation met on the matter, and they sent for Abba Moses, but he refused to come. Then they sent the priest of the church to him, saying, "Come. All the people are waiting for you." Moses got up and came.

He took a basket with a hole in it, filled it with sand, and carried it on his shoulders. Those who went out to meet him asked, "What does this mean, father?" He said the sand was "my sins, running down behind me. I cannot see them." And today, he said, he had come to judge faults that were not his own.

When they heard this, they set the brother free and said nothing more to him.

docstory-desert.story.sarah-answer.text: Amma Sarah is one of a few women the tradition remembers by name, and the Syriac collection keeps six sayings under her name. In the monks' speech, steadfast courage was called manly and weakness womanly. Amma Sarah used to say to her brothers, "It is I who am a man, and you who are women."

docstory-desert.story.antony-secret-buri.text:
Athanasius writes that Antony visited the monks of the outer mountain and told them it was his last visit. He said he would be surprised if they met again in this life, and that he was near a hundred and five years old.

The monks begged him to stay and die among them, but he would not, and above all for one reason. The Egyptians wrapped the bodies of good men in linen and kept them on couches in their houses. Antony had often urged the bishops to command the people against this, and he had taught that it was neither lawful nor holy.

He went back to the inner mountain, where he was used to living, and a few months later he fell sick. Two men had stayed with him there for fifteen years, serving him because of his age. He called them and told them to let no one take his body into Egypt. "Bury my body and hide it underground yourselves," he said. "Keep my words, so that no one may know the place but you alone."

He told them to divide his garments. One sheepskin and the garment he lay on were for the bishop Athanasius, and the other sheepskin was for the bishop Serapion. The two men were to keep the hair garment. Then he said farewell, and died.

They buried him as he had commanded, and Athanasius writes that to this day no one knows where he lies, except those two.

docstory-desert.story.sarapion-anthropom.text:
Cassian tells of an old monk named Sarapion, who lived at Scete and had kept a strict life there for a long time.

Then letters came from Theophilus, the bishop of Alexandria, refuting the belief that God has a human form. Almost all the monks of Egypt took them with great bitterness. At Scete, Cassian says, only Paphnutius, the presbyter of his own congregation, would allow the letter to be read.

Sarapion was one of those who held that belief. Paphnutius urged him many times, but to Sarapion the bishop's teaching seemed new, never handed down by his predecessors. Then a learned deacon named Photinus arrived from Cappadocia. Paphnutius asked him a question before all the brothers: how did the churches of the East read the words in Genesis, "Let us make man after our image and likeness"? Photinus answered that they took the words spiritually, not by the bare letters, and that God's glory could not be held in a human shape. At last the old man was shaken and agreed.

Cassian says they were all delighted. But as they rose to pray together, Sarapion felt the picture of God he used to set before himself in prayer leave his heart. He burst into bitter tears, threw himself on the ground, and cried out with deep groans: "Alas! I am a wretched man! They have taken my God away from me. Now I have no one to hold on to. I do not know whom to worship, or whom to address."

story.text:
From around 311, two rival churches stood side by side in Roman North Africa, centered on Carthage and Numidia. Both churches confessed one faith in the Trinity and in Christ, but they split over whether a bishop's conduct under persecution could void what his hand later gave. One side said it could. That side saw itself as the pure, persecuted church of the martyrs, the one true church. History calls its members Donatists, after an early bishop. Optatus, an opponent, says its bishops called themselves 'the party of Donatus' when questioned in court. Whether they used that name among themselves is not known.

The quarrel began in the persecution of 303 to 305, when officials demanded that clergy hand over the scriptures and the church's vessels to be destroyed. Some did. Others refused and suffered for it. The Donatists held that what a minister did in that moment decided whether his hand could be trusted afterward. In 311 or 312, Caecilian was elected bishop of Carthage. Felix of Aptungi, who ordained him, was accused of handing over the scriptures. If that was true, the Donatists held, the new bishop was no bishop at all. A rival party made Majorinus bishop in his place. The emperor later had the charge against Felix tried. Under threat of torture, a witness admitted forging part of the evidence, and Felix was cleared.

For a century, anyone who crossed over from Caecilian's church, the one later known as the Catholic church, was washed again. The Donatists did not count it as a second baptism. In their view, a hand from a broken line had given nothing the first time. Imperial edicts named the practice as an offense.

In 347 and 348 the emperor's commissioners came to force the two churches into one, this time at the urging of Caecilian's church. The Donatists called it persecution. Their own account says that Bishop Marculus was held four days at a cliff called Novapetra. There, it says, he fasted and was shown a vision of a cup, a crown and a palm, and then he was thrown down. Two laymen of Carthage, Isaac and Maximianus, were flogged and sunk in the sea. Every year, at the grave, the Donatists read such accounts aloud.

By the later fourth century the Donatist church was a full parallel church, with its own bishops, basilicas and councils in the same towns as Caecilian's church. In Numidia it far outnumbered Caecilian's church, and there it was the ordinary church of the village.

Optatus also reports that their bishop Donatus once asked what the emperor had to do with the church. The hearing at Rome in 313 and the Council of Arles in 314 ruled against the Donatists, and they rejected both rulings. In their view, a council called and enforced by a state that already favored Caecilian's church was not the church judging itself. Still, three times they turned to the state when that served their case. They petitioned Constantine in 313 and Julian in 361, and in the 390s they invoked imperial law against their own breakaway Maximianists.

At the Conference of Carthage in 411, about two hundred and eighty Donatist bishops faced a slightly larger number of bishops from Caecilian's church. The imperial judge offered them chairs, and they refused. Christ had stood before his governor, said Petilian, one of their speakers, and so would they. The judge granted that the name Catholic belonged to whichever side held the truth. But then he said he was bound by an imperial rescript that had already given the name to Caecilian's church. He ruled against the Donatists, and penal laws followed.

In 439 a Vandal army took Carthage. That removed the Roman power the Donatists had defined themselves against, but the contest went on under the Vandals, and then under the emperors of the East. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote of rebaptism still going on in Numidia and pressed for an inquiry.

Almost everything known about the Donatists was written by two men arguing against them, and most of their own words survive only as quotations in those men's books. Four short texts speak for them directly, and so do their bishops at the hearing of 411. So do two words cut into pillars near Bagai, Deo laudes, praise to God.

legacy.text:
Tyconius wrote the Book of Rules. A council of his own Donatist party is reported to have condemned him, but the book lasted longer than that party. It passed to Caecilian's church, the one later known as the Catholic church, and it shaped how Augustine read Scripture.

The contest between the two churches did not end in 439. It went on under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for about another century and a half. In the 590s Pope Gregory the Great wrote letters pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism still going on in Numidia. No line from the Donatists to any church a person could visit today has ever been shown.

docstory-don.story.council-of-cirta.text:
Before the quarrel over Caecilian began, the bishops of Numidia met at Cirta to make a bishop of their own. The year is disputed, 305 or 307 or later. Optatus tells the story of that meeting in his books against the Donatists.

Secundus of Tigisis presided. He asked whether any of them had handed over the scriptures in the persecution, and one by one, several said they had. It was the same charge the Donatists would soon bring against Felix, the bishop who made Caecilian.

Then Purpurius turned the question back on Secundus. He taunted him for being let go only after a long time among the soldiers. The room began to mutter that Secundus too had given up the sacred books to buy his release.

Secundus asked advice from his brother's son, called Secundus the Less, who told him to leave the whole affair to God. Secundus then asked the three bishops who had not been accused for their judgment. They were Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium and Nabor of Centurio, and they said a case like this should be reserved to the Lord.

"Sit down, all," Secundus said. "Thanks be to God," the assembly answered, and sat. No one was found guilty, and no one was cleared.

docstory-don.story.lucilla-affair.text:
She kept the bone of a martyr with her, and she kissed it before she took the cup at communion. Lucilla was a wealthy laywoman of Carthage, and the archdeacon Caecilian rebuked her for it. Optatus wrote against the Donatists about fifty years later. He adds that the dead man was not yet a recognized martyr, if he was one at all. She left, he says, full of anger.

Around then, persecution broke over Carthage, and the bishop, Mensurius, was summoned to the emperor's court. He left the church's gold and silver with elders he trusted. He gave an old woman a written list of it, to hand to whoever sat in the bishop's chair if he did not come home.

He did not come home. Botrus and Celestius had both expected the office, but Caecilian was elected instead. Optatus says the elders had kept back more of the treasure than they should have. In his telling, the elders, the two passed-over men and Lucilla now found a common cause.

At a crowded meeting in the basilica, Caecilian demanded that his accusers state their charge. Purpurius only mocked him. Let his head be well beaten in penance, he said. No proof was produced, and instead Majorinus, a member of Lucilla's household, was made bishop in Caecilian's place. It was done at her urging and through her bribes, Optatus writes.

docstory-don.story.acta-purgationis-feli.text:
At the center of the case lay a letter to Felix, the bishop of Aptungi who had made Caecilian bishop of Carthage. The Donatists said Felix had handed over the scriptures in the persecution. If that was true, they held, he had no right to make anyone a bishop, and Caecilian's office was void from its first day. The letter's closing lines seemed to prove it.

The emperor Constantine ordered the charge looked into, and the proconsul Aelianus heard named witnesses on the record. Their words survive in the dossier of documents kept by Optatus, an opponent of the Donatists. The letter came from a magistrate, Caecilianus. He told the court he had never dictated its closing lines.

Then a town official named Ingentius was questioned. Under the threat of torture, he broke. He admitted that he had added to the letter himself, out of grief over Maurus, his guest. A counsel named Apronianus charged that Ingentius had traveled through Numidia and Mauritania as the Donatist party's agent. Ingentius denied that he had been to Numidia.

The proconsul ruled that nothing had been proved against Felix, and he cleared him.

docstory-don.story.gesta-apud-zenophilum.text:
In 320 a Roman official named Zenophilus asked what had become of the church's money. The charge came from Nundinarius, a deacon whom his own bishop had demoted. Optatus, an opponent of the Donatists, kept the court record among his documents, because its findings tell against them.

The charge named Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, as a betrayer and a thief of the goods of the poor. It said the noble woman Lucilla had given four hundred pieces of silver. For that money, it said, the clergy had plotted to make Majorinus bishop, and the split came out of it.

Then letters were read aloud. Purpurius, a bishop, urged Silvanus to settle with the deacon quietly, before a flame broke out that could not be put out without spiritual bloodshed. In the same letter he said he knew the charges were true. A bishop named Fortis wrote that they should not go into a public court and be condemned by pagans. Several of the letters end the same way. Let no one know about it.

Then a witness named Victor was questioned. Had Silvanus handed anything over? He had, Victor said, but not in his presence. Victor said he had fought against making Silvanus bishop, and when pressed to confess what he knew, he said it plainly. "He was a betrayer."

docstory-don.story.passio-marculi.text:
The Donatists remembered Marculus as a man who had already turned from worldly advancement and given his life to the church. Their account of his suffering, the Passio Marculi, names no author. It gives a day but no year.

In the Passio's telling, when Macarius's persecution came into Numidia, ten Donatist bishops were sent to meet him, and Marculus was among them. It says he was seized at Vegesela, bound to columns and flogged, and that he bore it without visible pain and praised God the whole time. Then he was paraded through several towns of Numidia and held four days at a cliff called Novapetra.

There, the account says, he fasted and was given a vision. A cup, a crown and a palm were shown to him together, and before dawn he was thrown from the cliff.

The Donatists held that his body did not break in the fall. It came down gently, they said, as though something carried it. A bright cloud covered it, and flashes of light showed the brothers where he lay, so that they could take him for burial.

docstory-don.story.macrobius-letter.text:
Maximianus, a soldier of Christ in the letter's words, was chosen to face the Roman proconsul first. The Donatist bishop Macrobius told the story in a letter to the people of Carthage. In it, the night before, at a shared meal, the wine in Maximianus's cup seemed to take the shape of a crown. It shone with the colors of blood and light, and Macrobius took it as an omen of what the next day would ask.

Maximianus was beaten with leaded whips and then with rods, and Isaac was flogged beside him. Isaac called his floggers traditores, men who had handed over the scriptures, and told them to come and heal their madness of unity. Both men were sentenced to exile and shut in prison, and there Isaac died.

That night, Macrobius writes, Maximianus dreamed he fought the emperor's officials and then the emperor himself, and struck out his eye. Then a bright youth crowned him. The proconsul wanted neither man honored as a relic, so he had both bodies weighted with jars of sand and thrown into the sea. By the letter's account, Maximianus was still alive.

In Macrobius's account, the sea would not keep them. For six days, he says, the bodies were driven back toward the shore, until they came up whole to the people waiting. Macrobius closes by telling his readers that the two martyrs wait for them with arms stretched out from heaven, and he urges the living to hurry after them.

docstory-don.story.tyconius-condemnation.text:
Tyconius argued at length, with strong support from Scripture, that the Christians of Africa belonged to a church spread across the whole earth. Anyone who followed the case could see where it led. If he was right, the African churches still in communion with the rest had lost nothing by staying. Those who had left that communion, his own Donatist party among them, had broken away from something real.

Parmenian, the Donatist bishop at Carthage, saw where the argument pointed, and he did not follow it. Augustine, writing against the Donatists some twenty years later, tells what came next. Parmenian wrote to Tyconius and rebuked him for preaching that the church spread across the whole earth. He warned him never to dare do it again.

Tyconius did not take it back, and he did not leave. He went on arguing from inside the party that had told him to stop. It is reported, Augustine says, that a council of his own communion then condemned him. He never went over to Caecilian's church, the one later known as the Catholic church.

docstory-don.story.bagai-reconciliation.text:
In 393 a deacon named Maximian was made rival primate at Cebarsussi, against Primian, the Donatist primate at Carthage. In miniature, it was the act the Donatist founders had once taken against Caecilian.

The answer came the next year at Bagai. Three hundred and ten Donatist bishops met there and condemned the followers of Maximian in the harshest terms they had. Augustine quotes the decree word for word in his books against the Donatists. It calls them shipwrecked men, dashed by the waves of truth onto the sharp rocks. Their bodies cover the shore, it says, and they cannot even find a grave.

Later the Donatist party took back two of those condemned bishops, Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuris. Neither was baptized again or ordained again. Optatus Gildonianus, one of the Donatist bishops, used soldiers to enforce their return.

These two had baptized while in schism, and Augustine made this the center of his case against the Donatists. If their baptisms could stand on Donatist authority, he argued, then the Donatist rule did not hold even for the Donatists themselves.

docstory-don.story.conference-of-carthag.text:
The judge sat, and the Donatist bishops stood. Flavius Marcellinus offered them chairs, and said it weighed on him to sit while so many venerable men stood. Petilian thanked him and refused. He and his fellow bishops did not blush and did not fear, he said. Christ himself stood before the governor, so how could they refuse to stand?

This was Carthage in the summer of 411. The emperor had ordered the whole quarrel settled at law, and imperial notaries took down what was said.

Emeritus of Caesarea carried the Donatist argument. He would not let the court touch the case itself until it had settled the day, the mandates and who was bringing the charge. When the bishops of Caecilian's church claimed the name Catholic, Petilian answered that it meant nothing until the case was decided. Marcellinus agreed that the name belonged to whichever side the truth was found with. But then he said he was bound by the emperor's written order, which had already given them that name.

On the third day Augustine argued from the wheat and the weeds that the church holds good and bad together. Emeritus answered him verse for verse from the same books. He signed the notary's record of most of what he said, and at times he added that he kept his right to appeal.

In the end Marcellinus ruled against the Donatists, though the printed acts break off before his sentence.

story.text:
In Roman Gaul, between about 360 and 450 CE, two households of monks lived out the same idea. In both, a monk who was made a bishop went on living as a monk. One grew up in the north, around Tours, in the Loire valley. The other grew up in the south, on Lérins, a small island off the Mediterranean coast, and in the city of Marseilles. No evidence shows that the two ever wrote to each other.

The northern household began with a soldier named Martin. Before a battle, he asked his commander, Julian Caesar, for his discharge, to serve Christ instead. Years later the people of Tours drew him out of his monastery by a trick and made him their bishop. As bishop, Martin kept the plain habits of a monk, and many of the monks he trained were later made bishops.

After Martin's death, Honoratus took his followers to Lérins. The island stood empty, because it was filthy and no one went near it for fear of snakes. His disciple Hilary preached that Honoratus went in unafraid, with a psalm on his lips, and the snakes gave way. As far as Hilary's sermon can be read, the priesthood he had run from caught up with him on the island, and in time he became a bishop himself.

Both households measured themselves against Egypt's monks, in different ways. The south took Egypt's customs as a rule to keep. John Cassian had lived among the Egyptian monks and brought their customs home to Gaul. He changed them only where Gaul's harsh climate or different habits made them impossible or too hard. The north set Martin beside Egypt's hermits. The Tours writer Sulpitius has a traveler just back from Egypt admit that Martin had outdone them all.

From the fathers of Egypt, the south received a goal called purity of heart, and fasting and night prayer were only aids toward it. Discretion, the judgment that keeps a monk between too much and too little, kept him on course, and the Egyptian fathers called it the mother of all virtues. On Lérins, Vincent wrote that the true faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.

In his Institutes, Cassian chose not to write up the wonders he had seen, since they teach nothing about how to live. In his Conferences, an Egyptian elder says the fathers never counted a monk good if he showed off his power over demons. Tours, by contrast, told its story through power. Sulpitius tells how Martin brought a dead catechumen, a new believer not yet baptized, back to life. He also tells how the devil once came to Martin dressed as Christ. Martin refused him, saying he would believe only in a Christ who bore the marks of his wounds.

By Cassian's own account, the south's best-known argument began as a worry at prayer. In Egypt, an old man named Chaeremon told Cassian and his friend Germanus that no one masters the good by effort alone. When Germanus objected, Chaeremon answered with a farmer. A farmer who never plows gets no crop, yet even the hardest worker needs rain he cannot make. The wish to do good, the old man said, comes first from God. That answer grew into a whole Conference on grace and effort.

At Tours, some bishops had opposed Martin's election. Later, at the emperor's court in Trier, Martin once took communion with bishops he had refused, to save lives. He felt it cost him some of his power, and he never attended a synod again. Vincent, by contrast, wrote that the decrees of an ancient general council should be preferred to the rashness and ignorance of a few.

Almost everything known about Tours comes from Sulpitius Severus, who visited Martin there. He was not present for most of what he tells, and says he learned it from Martin and those who lived with him.
