Knowing his end was near, Martin went to make peace among the quarreling clergy at Condate. As he lay dying, his monks asked to put straw under him, but he kept to sackcloth and ashes, so as not to leave them a different example. Almost two thousand monks, it is said, came to his funeral.

legacy.text: After 450 the argument over grace and effort went on, but it was no longer one monk writing to another. In the 470s Faustus, once abbot of Lérins and by then a bishop, took it up. He says he wrote at the request of church councils at Arles and Lyons, as a bishop writing for other bishops.

docstory-gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amien.text:
Martin's father was a tribune, an army officer. When Martin was fifteen, his father informed on him, and he was seized, put in chains and made to swear the soldier's oath. Even then he kept only one servant, and Martin was the one who served, pulling off his servant's boots and cleaning them himself. He was still a catechumen, preparing for baptism, and he kept from his pay only what each day required.

One winter was so harsh that many people were dying of the cold. At the gate of Amiens, Martin met a poor man with no clothes at all, and everyone passed him by. Martin had nothing left but his weapons and his cloak, so he drew his sword, cut the cloak in two, and gave half to the beggar. Some onlookers laughed at him, while others were ashamed, because they had more than he did and had never done anything like it.

That night, Sulpitius says, Martin saw Christ in his sleep, wearing the half he had given away. Christ told the angels around him that Martin, still only a catechumen, had clothed him. Martin did not grow proud, and he went and was baptized at twenty. His commander, a tribune who shared his tent, promised to leave the world with him once his own command ended. So Martin stayed nearly two more years, a soldier in name only.

docstory-gallic.story.discharge-before-c.text:
Barbarians were pushing into Gaul, and Julian Caesar had gathered his army to meet them. He was handing out a donative, a gift of money, and calling his soldiers forward one by one. When Martin's turn came, he would not take the money. He had served Caesar long enough, he said, and now he asked to serve God, since, as Christ's soldier, he could not lawfully fight.

Julian, whom Sulpitius calls the tyrant, said Martin was running from the coming battle out of fear. The charge only made Martin firmer. If this was cowardice, he said, he would stand before the enemy line the next day with no weapon, and the sign of the cross would be his only protection. He was sent back to prison to wait for morning.

The next day the enemy sent envoys to ask for peace. Sulpitius says God was sparing Martin the sight of other men dying. The enemy gave up themselves and everything they had, and no battle was fought.

docstory-gallic.story.raising-of-the-cat.text:
Martin had set up a monastery for himself not far from the town. A catechumen, a man still preparing for baptism, came to live with him and learn from his teaching and his life. Within a few days the man fell ill with fever. Martin was away for three days, and when he came back the man was dead, so suddenly that he had never been baptized.

As Sulpitius tells it, Martin sent everyone out of the cell, bolted the door and stretched himself full length on the body. He prayed, and when he sensed that power was present, he rose and waited for the Lord's mercy. Within two hours the dead man began to stir and opened his eyes. Martin cried out his thanks so loudly that the brothers rushed in and found alive the man they had left dead. He was baptized at once and lived for many years.

The man himself used to tell what had happened to him, Sulpitius says. He had stood before the Judge and been sent to a gloomy place among common crowds. Then two angels said that he was the man Martin was praying for, and he was given back to Martin. From that day, people counted Martin holy, powerful and truly apostolic.

docstory-gallic.story.election-at-tours.text:
The people of Tours wanted Martin as their bishop, but Sulpitius says he could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. So a citizen named Ruricius knelt before him and pretended that his wife was sick. When Martin came out to help, citizens lining the road led him into the city as if under guard. A huge crowd from Tours and the nearby towns had gathered to vote, and nearly all of them wanted Martin.

A few people objected, among them some of the bishops called in to consecrate him. Led by a bishop named Defensor, they said Martin looked contemptible, with his shabby clothes and disgusting hair. The crowd only laughed.

That day the reader could not get through the crowd, and while the officials stood confused, someone picked up the psalter and read the first verse he found. Out of the mouths of babes and infants, it said, God had perfected praise, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. The crowd roared, and Defensor's side fell silent, for people believed God had chosen the verse as a witness against him. Martin became bishop of Tours, and as bishop he kept the dignity of the office and the plain habits of a monk.

docstory-gallic.story.trier-and-the-itha.text:
This story comes from Gallus, one of Martin's disciples, in Sulpitius's Dialogues. Martin never told it outside his own household.

After Priscillian was put to death, the emperor Maximus protected Ithacius, the bishop who had accused him, and the bishops gathered at Trier stood by Ithacius. Maximus was about to send tribunes, officers with power over life and death, into Spain to hunt down heretics. Martin came to court and begged that none be sent, to spare the heretics as well as the true Christians. In his Sacred History, Sulpitius tells of an earlier stage, before Priscillian's death. There he says Martin held it a shocking wrong for a worldly ruler to judge a church case.

The bishops begged Maximus to turn against Martin, and Maximus ordered death for the people Martin had defended. Martin hurried to the palace that night and promised to take communion with the bishops if those lives were spared and the tribunes called back. Maximus agreed. The next day, when a bishop named Felix was ordained, Martin took communion, yet he would never put his name to it in writing.

Leaving the city, he sat alone in the woods near the village of Andethanna, torn with grief. Gallus says an angel came and told him his remorse was just, though he had no other way out. Afterward his healing sometimes came more slowly, and with tears Martin blamed that one communion. Gallus says he lived sixteen more years and never went to a synod again.

docstory-gallic.story.brictio-in-the-cou.text:
One day, as his disciple Gallus tells it, Martin sat on his wooden seat, the one Gallus's listeners all knew, in the little court outside his door. Gallus says Martin saw two demons on the rock above the monastery, calling out with glee, "Come here, Brictio, come here, Brictio." Then Brictio burst in, raging.

Brictio was a presbyter, a priest, whom Martin had raised in the monastery from boyhood. The day before, Martin had rebuked him, because Brictio had owned nothing when he joined the clergy and was now buying horses and slaves. Many said the slaves included boys bought from beyond the frontier and girls chosen for their looks. Pale with fury, Brictio claimed he was the holier man, since he had grown up in the Church while Martin had been a soldier. He called Martin's visions ridiculous fancies and nearly struck him, but Martin answered him gently.

Brictio stormed out, sure he had won, but soon he came back, threw himself at Martin's feet and begged for pardon, admitting that a demon had taken hold of him. Martin forgave him easily. Afterward, whenever Brictio was accused of serious wrongs, Martin would not remove him, because he did not want anyone to think he was avenging an insult to himself. If Christ bore with Judas, he would ask, why should he not bear with Brictio?

docstory-gallic.story.death-of-martin-at.text:
Martin had long known when he would die, Sulpitius writes, and he had told the brothers so. When the clergy at Condate fell to quarreling, he went to make peace among them, judging that one more church at peace would be a fitting end to his life.

Peace was made, but as he was about to return to the monastery, his strength failed. The brothers wept and begged him not to leave them, and Martin wept too. He prayed that he would not refuse more work if he was still needed, and he left the choice to God.

For some days he lay in fever on sackcloth and ashes, praying through whole nights. His disciples asked to put some ordinary straw under him, but he refused. A Christian should die among ashes, he said, and he would be sinning if he left them a different example. Those who were there told Sulpitius that Martin saw the devil standing near and rebuked him without fear. Then he died, and they said his face looked like an angel's.

The whole city his body was brought to poured out to meet it, with people from the villages and towns around. Almost two thousand monks, it is said, came to his funeral. Old men walked with young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins kept their grief hidden.

docstory-gallic.story.the-angel-and-the-.text:
Cassian brought this story to Gaul from the fathers of Egypt. In the earliest days, they say, only a few men were called monks, and they were the best of men. They lived like the first believers in Jerusalem, with one heart and one soul and everything shared. The elder fathers met to set a daily rule of prayer for those who would come after them.

Each father thought only of his own strength and proposed the number of psalms that suited him. Some wanted fifty, some sixty and some still more, and they were still arguing when the hour for evening prayer came.

So they stopped to pray. One father rose to sing while the rest sat listening, and he sang eleven psalms, each followed by a prayer. Then he ended the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished from their sight. The fathers saw Providence at work, for through an angel, they believed, a rule had been fixed for every community of brothers. From then on they kept twelve psalms at the evening and night prayers, and later they added two readings of their own choosing.

docstory-gallic.story.germanus-scruple-a.text:
Cassian wrote this down years later, in Gaul. He and his friend Germanus had spent an evening in Egypt, at the cell of an old man named Chaeremon near Panephysis, hearing him teach on chastity. One sentence troubled Germanus. The old man had said that even striving with all one's might cannot make a person master of the good, and that it must be received as a gift.

They slept a little and came back for morning prayer, still whispering about it. Chaeremon noticed, cut the service short and asked what was wrong.

Germanus said that chastity is won by long, hard toil, and that the credit should go mainly to the one who does the work, as a farmer earns his harvest. Chaeremon answered that no farmer can claim his harvest by his labor alone, because he needs rain he cannot control. Yet God gives no rich crop to a farmer who never plows. In the same way, the wish to do good and the chance to do it both come first from God. The human part, he said, is to follow day by day the grace that draws a person on.

Later in the same Conference, Chaeremon says that grace works together with the human will, and sometimes waits for some effort from it. Elsewhere he says that wanting the good, doing it and holding on to it are all God's gifts. Yet none of them takes away free will, and how both can be true, he says, the human mind cannot fully grasp.

docstory-gallic.story.honoratus-and-the-.text:
When Honoratus, the founder of the monastery on Lérins, died, his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life. Honoratus, Hilary says, left his homeland because he longed for the desert. An island stood empty, because it was filthy and no one could go near it for fear of poisonous snakes. He was drawn there by the chance of solitude, and by the nearness of the holy bishop Leontius, whom he loved. Many people tried to hold him back by warning him how terrible the place was, but he wanted to be cut off from the world, even by the sea.

He carried a psalm in his heart and on his lips. It promised that he would tread on the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the dragon. So he went in unafraid, Hilary says, and his calm scattered the fear of his own people. The horror of the empty place fled, and the snakes gave way. Snakes were often met in those parts, Hilary adds, yet they never harmed or even frightened anyone, and he counts this among his master's miracles.

There Honoratus set up a camp of God. And there, as far as Hilary's sermon can be read, the priesthood caught up with the man who had run from it. He was made a presbyter, a priest, and he kept a monk's humility inside the priesthood.

story.text:
This is the story of one circle, from 382 to 420 CE, in Rome and in Bethlehem. In 382 a scholar named Jerome reached Rome as secretary and scriptural adviser to Pope Damasus. There he met a household that already existed. The widow Marcella had made her house on the Aventine hill a place of fasting and scripture study, and historians think other women had joined her before Jerome came. He brought what the household lacked, a scholar's training in texts.

The women of the circle gave up wealth, marriage prospects and rank on purpose, as devotion to Christ. For them, this giving up was itself how a Christian life took shape. Jerome says Marcella turned down a rich suitor and chose a plain life.

In 384 Blaesilla, the daughter of the widow Paula, died in Rome at about twenty. She had been widowed young and had taken up a severe ascetic discipline only months before. Jerome reports that the funeral crowd said fasting had killed her, and that they asked why the detestable monks were not stoned or thrown into the Tiber. That December Pope Damasus died, and the protection he had given Jerome ended with him. In August 385 Jerome sailed east. From the ship he wrote that all Rome had praised him before he knew Paula's house, and that now he was called infamous.

Paula followed him east and settled in Bethlehem. She founded a community of women there and led it until she died in 404. Jerome writes that her fortune paid for houses for monks and for virgins, and for a hostel for travelers. Jerome himself was only a presbyter, under the bishop of Jerusalem. After Paula's death her daughter Eustochium led the women.

Jerome held that the Hebrew text of scripture stood closest to what God said, closer than the Greek version the church had long used. At Bethlehem he spent years turning the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew, book by book. Nearly every book came with a short, fighting preface that defended his choices against critics. By Jerome's account, Paula's fortune also paid for his Hebrew teachers.

Around 403, in the North African town of Oea, a bishop read the prophet Jonah aloud from the new translation. The familiar version said a gourd had shaded the prophet, but the new one said ivy, and the congregation erupted. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, told Jerome what happened. According to Augustine, the bishop of Oea was close to losing his people, so he asked the town's Jewish residents about the Hebrew. They backed the old word, and the bishop corrected the reading. Augustine feared that setting aside the old Greek text would put the church's unity at risk, and he wrote that the story made him think Jerome might sometimes be mistaken. Jerome answered point by point. Neither man conceded, and their courteous letters kept crossing for years.

Marcella stayed in Rome. Jerome wrote after her death that, once he left, people in Rome brought their disputes about scripture to her to settle. Many men put hard questions to her, he adds, and priests were sometimes among them. She gave her answers as if they came from him or someone else. In 410 Alaric's Goths took Rome. As Jerome heard it, soldiers came to Marcella's house demanding gold. They did not believe her when she pointed to her plain dress, and they beat her. She died a few days later.

In 416 a quarrel over the teaching of Pelagius reached the Bethlehem monasteries as an attack. Pope Innocent wrote that Eustochium and her young niece, also named Paula, had reported murders and fires to him. He added that they would not name the man behind it. Jerome wrote that the Bethlehem house had lost its earthly wealth but was still filled with spiritual riches.

Jerome died in 420, by the accepted count. Eustochium died in 418, 419 or 420. Years later Augustine called Jerome a most learned man who had translated the scriptures from the Hebrew, and he granted that even the Jews called the work faithful. Still, he said, the churches of Christ judged that no one should be preferred to the authority of the Septuagint translators.

legacy.text:
The circle's own record does not follow Jerome's central labor past his lifetime. It shows an argument that was still open when he died.

Within a few years, a respected fellow scholar, Augustine, made the strongest case for the other side, in writing. He agreed with every point of the Hebrew scholarship, yet he still refused the conclusion. The churches of Christ, he wrote, should trust the old Greek translators, not one modern scholar's own work, however sound.

Did the Hebrew-based translation ever become the circle's own settled Bible? Its surviving writings cannot answer that question. They end with the argument still unresolved.

docstory-hal.story.ciceronian-dream.text:
On the road to Jerusalem, Jerome could give up everything except his library. So he said in a letter meant to teach, and he told the story against himself.

He fasted, and then he read Cicero. He wept over his sins, and then he took up Plautus again. When he made himself go back to the prophets, their style seemed crude to him, and it repelled him.

Then a fever took him, so deep that his funeral was being prepared. In spirit, he said, he was dragged before the judgment seat. Asked who he was, he answered that he was a Christian, but the Judge told him that he lied. You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ, the Judge said, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

Jerome said he was flogged, and his conscience burned worse than the lash. He swore an oath that if he ever again owned worldly books, he would have denied his Lord. He woke with his eyes drenched. From then on, he wrote, he read the divine books with more zeal than he had ever given to the books of men.

His enemies, Rufinus among them, later mocked him over the dream and the oath. They pointed out that his pages never stopped quoting the classics.

docstory-hal.story.marcella-standing.text:
A widow on the Aventine hill in Rome once turned down a rich old suitor. If she had wished to marry again, she told him, she would have looked for a husband, not an inheritance.

Her standing survives in one man's memorial. Jerome wrote it when she was two years dead, and her letters to him are lost.

When Jerome came to Rome, she pressed him with questions on scripture until his reluctance gave way. She never took an answer without disputing it, he wrote. Her aim, he said, was to learn what could be said against his answers. His own letters show that she asked hard questions, and more than a dozen of his surviving answers were written to her.

After he left for Bethlehem, the memorial says, people turned to her when a dispute about scripture arose in Rome, and she settled it. Many men brought her hard questions, he adds, and priests were sometimes among them. She gave her opinions as if they came from him or from someone else, not from herself. In this, he says, she was mindful of the apostle's rule.

Later, in his telling, Marcella was the one who set in motion the condemnation of the heretics in Rome.

docstory-hal.story.paula-epitaph.text:
Paula's own voice was not kept. She survives in the memorial Jerome wrote, and it is told here as the ideal that memorial teaches.

Paula came from the oldest blood in Rome, and she counted the Gracchi in her family line. She was a wife and mother in the grandest style the city knew. Then her husband died, and she changed. She wept so hard, Jerome wrote, that she nearly died of grief, and then she turned that whole ruined love toward God.

She dressed plainly and slept on the ground. She gave until she was borrowing to give more, the memorial says. She left Rome for a cave-town in Palestine, and her children stood on the shore. There, Jerome writes, her fortune built houses for monks, for virgins and for strangers on the road. She led her women in psalms and in scripture, and she learned Hebrew well enough to chant the psalms in it. She nursed the sick with her own hands.

She left her daughter a mass of debt, her memorial says, and faith as her only wealth. When she died, bishops carried her body, and the memorial says the whole population of Palestine's cities came. Paula was laid beneath the church at the place of the Lord's birth.

docstory-hal.story.rome-crisis.text:
Blaesilla was Paula's daughter, widowed young, and she took up the ascetic discipline with a convert's fire. Within months she was dead, at about twenty years old.

At the funeral, Paula collapsed and was carried fainting through the procession. Jerome reports what the crowd began to mutter. See what comes of their fasting, they said, and she weeps for a daughter killed by it. How long, they asked, before we drive these detestable monks out of Rome, stone them and throw them into the Tiber?

That winter the old pope, Damasus, died. In Jerome's telling, the pope had been his shelter, and with him gone the whispers became open slander.

Within the year, Jerome stood on a ship at Ostia, writing a last letter to a friend. Before he knew Paula's house, he wrote, all Rome had praised him, and now he was called infamous. He sailed east, and Paula followed.

docstory-hal.story.journey-to-bethlehem.text:
Paula went down to the harbor at Portus, and her children stood on the shore. Jerome's memorial of her says her eyes were dry and lifted toward heaven as the ship pulled out, while her little son stretched out his hands from the beach.

She sailed east by way of Cyprus, where the bishop Epiphanius kept her for ten days, and went on to Antioch. Then she traveled the whole length of the holy places, with scripture in hand at every stop. At the cave in Bethlehem she wept, Jerome says. In his telling, she greeted the town by name, the house of bread, where the Bread from heaven was born.

She went on into Egypt, to Nitria, where the bishop Isidore came out to meet her with a great crowd of monks. Paula wished to press deeper into the desert and stay among the monks' settlements, but she turned back to Bethlehem instead. She lived in a poor lodging at first. Then, Jerome writes, she lived for the rest of her life in the monasteries her fortune built.

docstory-hal.story.rufinus-rupture.text:
Jerome and Rufinus had been friends since their student days. Both had lived the ascetic life as young men, and both admired the great teacher Origen and translated his works.

Then Origen's boldest ideas came under condemnation. One was that souls lived before birth, and another concerned the shape of the body at the resurrection. Every admirer of Origen had to answer for that admiration.

Rufinus translated Origen's great work, and in its preface he wrote that he was only following the method of a respected predecessor. He named no one, but everyone knew he meant Jerome.

Each man wrote a formal defense, and both defenses survive. They used each other's old writings as weapons. Both claimed the catholic faith, and each said the other had betrayed it. Friends tried to reconcile them, and the bishop of Rome was drawn in, but the break was never repaired.

docstory-hal.story.oea-gourd.text:
In Oea, a town in North Africa, a bishop read the prophet Jonah to his congregation from Jerome's new translation. In the old, familiar version, God's plant shading the prophet was a gourd. The new version gave a different word, ivy.

The congregation erupted, and the Greeks among them corrected the reader aloud and called the translation false. Close to losing his people, the bishop asked the town's Jewish residents about the Hebrew. They sided with the old version, whether from ignorance or spite, as Augustine reports it, and the bishop corrected the reading.

Augustine sent the story across the sea to Bethlehem. He said it made him think Jerome might sometimes be mistaken.

Jerome answered him point by point. The Hebrew word, he said, named a shrub that was neither gourd nor ivy. He had chosen ivy, he wrote, so as not to differ from the other translators. If the Jews had said otherwise, he wrote, they were ignorant or mocking.

Neither man gave way, and their letters kept crossing for years.

docstory-hal.story.marcella-death.text:
The Goths broke into Rome, and at last their soldiers came to Marcella's house on the Aventine. Far away in Bethlehem, Jerome later wrote down what he had heard of that day.

The old woman met the soldiers, his account says, without a look of alarm. They demanded her gold, and she pointed to her coarse dress, but they did not believe her. They beat her with clubs, though she is said to have felt no pain. She threw herself at their feet in tears and begged them not to take from her the young woman in her care.

Something in the scene moved even those men, the account says. They took the two women to the basilica of the apostle Paul, where they might find safety, or at least a tomb.

In the basilica, it is said, Marcella thanked God that the young woman was unharmed. She was thankful too, the account says, that the taking of the city had found her poor, and had not made her poor. After a few days, she died.

docstory-hal.story.attack-416.text:
In 416, men attacked the monasteries at Bethlehem. The violence came from fellow Christians, out of the Pelagian controversy. The surviving letters speak of ravages, murders, fires and outrages of every kind, and of buildings burned.

Jerome wrote afterward, briefly, that his monastery had been destroyed. He had chosen to leave his pleasant home, he said, rather than give up the faith.

Eustochium and her young niece Paula wrote to Innocent, the bishop of Rome, and told him what had been done. Their letter is lost, and it is known only through his. The community never said who struck the blow, how many died, or what was lost.

Innocent wrote his sympathy to Jerome directly. He also wrote to the bishop of Jerusalem. In that letter he marveled that the women had declined to name the man behind the attack, and he rebuked the bishop for letting it happen.

story.text:
From 312 to 451, in Rome, Constantinople and Milan, the church fought over who had the last word. The emperor, a council and the bishop of Rome each had a claim. Three answers competed over what that authority rested on. Rome traced its standing to the apostle Peter, and Constantinople based its rank on being near the emperor. Ambrose of Milan held that a bishop's sacraments and moral standing gave him leverage over any ruler.

In 312 Constantine fought the battle at the Milvian Bridge. Eusebius tells what Constantine himself told him long afterward: about noon, he said, he saw a cross of light with the words "Conquer by this." His whole army, he said, saw it too. Lactantius wrote earlier and tells it differently: in his account a dream told Constantine to mark Christ's sign on his soldiers' shields. The empire stopped hunting the church, and within a year toleration was law.

A council in the East deposed Athanasius, the bishop of Alexandria, and in 341 Julius, bishop of Rome, wrote back that the custom was to write to Rome first. Those he wrote to disputed how old and settled that custom was.

Imperial favor did not stay with one creed. Under Constantius II the empire's own church confessed that the Son is like the Father, a creed called Homoian. Valens enforced it again in the East, and for roughly two decades it was the official faith. Bishops who held the Nicene faith were deposed and exiled.

Ambrose set a limit on the alliance. In 386 the imperial court wanted one of his churches for the Homoian confession it held, and it acted under a law of January 386 allowing Homoians to assemble for worship. The printed edition of Ambrose's letters dates the law a year earlier.

Ambrose refused to give the church up. "I cannot give up the basilica, but I must not fight," he told his sister. Soldiers stood around the building, and Ambrose stayed inside with the people.

Augustine, then in the city, remembered that they kept guard, ready to die with their bishop. He wrote that Milan then began to sing hymns and psalms in the Eastern way. Ambrose preached that the emperor is within the Church, not above it, and the court did not take the building.

In 388 Christians burned the synagogue at Callinicum, on the eastern frontier, and Theodosius ordered the local bishop to pay for a new one. Ambrose would not offer the sacrament until the emperor promised to change the order, and Theodosius gave in. Here Ambrose used his power to shield the people who set the fire.

In 390 a riot at Thessalonica killed one of the emperor's generals. Theodosius ordered revenge, and his soldiers killed a crowd in the circus with no trial. Theodoret writes that seven thousand are said to have died. Ambrose sent the emperor a private letter. "I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present," he wrote. He asked the emperor to repent before he stood at the altar again. Decades later, Sozomen and Theodoret wrote that the emperor did public penance.

Leo of Rome did not go to the council at Chalcedon in 451, but his legates went in his place, and his letter, the Tome, was read. The session record has the bishops crying out that Peter has spoken so through Leo.

Three weeks later the council passed Canon 28, which gave Constantinople privileges equal to old Rome's, and rank just after her. Earlier bishops, it said, had rightly given Rome privileges because it was the royal city, and the new royal city should be honored the same way.

Leo's legates objected, and Leo refused the canon. He wrote to the emperor that things secular stand on a different basis from things divine, and he said Constantinople was a royal city that could never be an apostolic see.

legacy.text:
The last council of this period did not close in agreement. Chalcedon's settlement on Christ's two natures was final for those who accepted it, but whole regions rejected it at once, starting in Egypt, at the council itself. This rejection did not fade the way earlier disputes had. It hardened into lasting division. The story of this period ends just as that fracture opens, and its documents say nothing of how the fracture would end.

The two rival claims argued over in this period have been argued over ever since. Does the record from this period already amount to a settled papacy, or is it a claim still being worked out? Later traditions still argue that question, from these same documents.

Constantinople's rank raises a second, related fight. The council at Chalcedon granted that rank on one ground: nearness to the throne, not an apostle's grave. The tradition that received the rank reads this one way, and the see that refused it reads it another way. These documents open that disagreement and do not close it.

docstory-ijc.story.dream-before-battle.text:
Lactantius tells the story of the Milvian Bridge differently, and he tells it earlier than Eusebius does. His account has no vision seen by daylight and no army of witnesses, and it has neither a standard carried before the troops nor words written across the sky.

In his telling, Constantine was directed in a dream to mark the heavenly sign on his soldiers' shields and so to go into battle. The sign was the letter mark that stands for Christ. Constantine did as he had been commanded, and by that mark, Lactantius says, his army won at the bridge.

docstory-ijc.story.vision-and-alliance.text:
Eusebius tells what Constantine himself told him, long afterward and under oath. While he was on campaign, about noon, Constantine said he saw with his own eyes a cross of light in the sky above the sun. It carried the words "Conquer by this." His whole army, he said, saw it too.

That night, Eusebius says, Christ appeared to Constantine in his sleep with the same sign. Christ commanded him to make a standard of it and to carry it before his armies. Constantine did so, and then came the battle at the Milvian Bridge.

Eusebius reports what a ruler wanted remembered about his own rise, and he wrote it after that ruler's death.

The empire stopped hunting the church, and within a year toleration was law.

docstory-ijc.story.emperor-builds-anothe.text:
When Constantine stepped into the quarrel in Africa's church, he did what emperors do and called a hearing. The matter had already been heard at Rome, but in 314 he sent Caecilian and his accusers to Arles, and the councils duly ruled against the Donatists.

It settled nothing. Sixteen years later, in 330, the Donatists still held basilicas that the Catholics said belonged to them. One of those buildings was a church that Constantine had built himself, for Catholic use.

He wrote to the bishops of Numidia about it, but he did not order the buildings seized and he did not send troops. He left the Donatists where they were. The Catholic bishops had asked for another site instead, and he granted it. He paid for a new church to be built there for the Catholics, once again at his own expense.

He also ordered that the Catholic lower clergy be freed again from forced public service, which the Donatists had maneuvered them into.

docstory-ijc.story.letter-that-outranked.text:
A council in the East had condemned Athanasius of Alexandria and removed him from office, and Julius, bishop of Rome, was expected to accept that decision. Instead he wrote back, questioning the council's right to settle the matter before Rome had heard it.

He put it to them as a question. "Are you unaware that the custom has been to write to us first, and then for a just decision to be passed from this place?" Julius had not attended their council, and those he wrote to disputed how old and settled that custom was.

docstory-ijc.story.altar-of-victory.text:
The altar of Victory stood in the Senate house in Rome. Constantius had it removed, Julian put it back, and Gratian removed it again.

In the year 384, Symmachus petitioned the young emperor to bring the altar back. He was prefect of Rome and the most eloquent voice of the old religion. Rome's ancient worship, he said, had guarded Rome's ancient greatness, and so great a secret could not be reached by one road alone.

Ambrose answered him twice in writing. A Christian emperor's state, Ambrose argued, may not fund what the faith knows to be false. What Symmachus called reverence for the past was, to Ambrose, the past's own long error.

The altar stayed removed.

docstory-ijc.story.vigil-in-basilica.text:
The imperial court wanted one of Milan's churches for the worship of its own confession, the one that said "like the Father" and no more. The court was acting under an imperial law of January 386, which let that confession assemble for worship. The printed edition of Ambrose's letters, however, dates the law a year earlier.

Ambrose would not give the church up. As he told his sister, "I cannot give up the basilica, but I must not fight."

Soldiers came and stood around the building, but Ambrose stayed inside with the people, and the people stayed with him. Augustine was in the city, and he remembered it plainly. The pious people, he wrote, kept guard in the church, ready to die with their bishop.

It was then, Augustine says, that Milan began to sing hymns and psalms in the manner of the Eastern churches. They sang so that the people would not waste away in the weariness of sorrow. He wrote that the custom was kept from then on, and that nearly all congregations across the world copied it.

In the middle of the standoff, Ambrose preached that "the Emperor is within the Church, not above it." The court did not take the building.

docstory-ijc.story.callinicum-synagogue.text:
At Callinicum, on the eastern frontier, Christians burned the town's synagogue, and it was reported that the local bishop had urged it. In a separate attack, monks burned a meeting house of the Valentinians.

Theodosius heard of it and ordered the usual remedy. The bishop would pay to rebuild the synagogue, and the monks would be punished.

Ambrose wrote to the emperor himself to get the order reversed. He did not deny the burning, but he judged it unbearable for a bishop to be forced to pay for a synagogue. He judged it worse that anyone should answer for burning the Valentinian house, which he likened to a heathen temple.

When the order stood, Ambrose preached in front of Theodosius in church. He refused to offer the sacrament until the emperor promised, then and there, to change the order and end the inquiry, and Theodosius gave in.

His refusal protected the people who set the fire, and they never had to pay for what they burned.

docstory-ijc.story.emperor-penance.text:
In the year 390, a riot in Thessalonica killed one of the emperor's generals. Theodoret writes that in his rage Theodosius ordered a reprisal. His soldiers massacred the crowd in the circus with no trial, cutting down innocent and guilty together. It is said, Theodoret adds, that seven thousand died.

Ambrose wrote to the emperor in his own hand, for his eyes alone, and says he chose private words over public ones. "I, I say, have no reason to charge you with defiance, but I have reason to fear," he wrote. "I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present."

He asked whether what is not allowed after one innocent person's blood is shed could be allowed after the blood of many. He wanted the emperor's repentance shown before he stood at the altar again.

Two church historians, Sozomen and Theodoret, say that Theodosius did repent. Decades later they tell the famous scene, in which the emperor lays aside his purple robes and weeps for his sin in the church at Milan.

docstory-ijc.story.eutropius-at-the-alta.text:
Eutropius was a eunuch who rose to be chamberlain to the emperor Arcadius, and in 399 he became the first eunuch ever made consul. With that power he obtained laws that cut off the church's ancient right of refuge, so that a fugitive at the altar could be taken.

Then he fell. He ran to the Great Church and took hold of the altar, the one protection he had himself destroyed, and the soldiers came for him.

The bishop, John, preached with Eutropius lying there, and in front of the man and the whole city he preached the emptiness of everything Eutropius had spent his life getting. Where is the consulship now, he asked, and where are the torches and the swarm of people who flattered him?

Then John turned on his own congregation, who wanted the man handed over. He told them they were servants of a crucified man who had said, forgive them. Yes, he granted, this is the man who abolished refuge here, and he has learned by experience what he did.

The emperor held the army off, but the protection did not last. Eutropius left the church and was taken, and later he was exiled and executed. John preached a second time, about that too.

docstory-ijc.story.tome-that-would-not-b.text:
Leo did not go to Chalcedon, but his legates went in his place, and his letter, the Tome, was read to the assembled bishops. The session record has them crying out, "This is the faith of the fathers," and then, "Peter has spoken thus through Leo."

Not every bishop was satisfied, and the Tome was questioned in session and compared with the teaching of Cyril.

Three weeks later, the same council did something else. It gave Constantinople equal privileges with old Rome and a rank just after her. It also gave Constantinople the right to ordain the chief bishops of three regions.

No apostle had taught there, and the canon gave a different reason. Earlier bishops had rightly granted privileges to old Rome as the royal city, and the new royal city should be honored the same way.

Leo's legates objected in the council itself. When word reached Leo, he refused to accept the canon and wrote to the emperor, the empress and the bishop of Constantinople. To the emperor he wrote that "things secular stand on a different basis from things divine." Constantinople was a royal city, he said, but it could never be an apostolic see.

story.text:
From 1517 to 1580, a reform grew out of Wittenberg. Martin Luther taught there at the university.

At the heart of this tradition sits a frightened conscience. The churches of this reform taught that the commandments lead a person to despair of his own powers, and that God's promise then comforts him. In their teaching, a sinner is freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, and the sacraments carry that promise. Baptism means the old self is drowned by daily sorrow and repentance, and absolution is given as though from God himself. They held that in the Supper Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, and they gave no explanation of how.

On 31 October 1517 Luther, a friar, wrote to Albrecht, the Archbishop of Mainz. Preachers were offering indulgences in the archbishop's name, to help build St. Peter's in Rome, and Luther was troubled by what their hearers now believed. He asked the archbishop to withdraw the instruction the preachers worked from, and he sent ninety-five statements for debate with it, the Ninety-Five Theses.

In 1518 Luther was summoned to Augsburg. By his own account, told years later at his table, he knelt before Cardinal Cajetan. He would not say the one word an Italian urged on him, Revoco, which means I recant.

In 1521 Luther stood before the Emperor and the Electors at the Diet of Worms. He told the story years afterward to his students at his own table. By his account, he would not take back his books of teaching, though he was willing to be corrected if he had been too violent in his books against opponents. By the same account, the next day he said he would accept instruction in everything except what touches Holy Scripture.

The reform ran ahead of its founder. In March 1522 Luther left the Wartburg, where he had been hidden since Worms, against the Elector's instruction to stay. Wittenberg was in disorder over how fast to sweep away the old forms of worship. Luther preached eight days running and told his congregation he saw no signs of love among them.

On 1 July 1523 two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after they refused to give up their teaching. Within months Luther wrote a ballad about them.

The reform also taught people in their own language. German hymns were sung inside the Mass. Wittenberg's first hymn-book was printed in 1524 and held eight hymns, four of them Luther's. Johann Walter later remembered that Luther kept him at Wittenberg for three weeks. Walter wrote out the notes for some of the Gospels and Epistles until the first German Mass was sung.

The reform's chief tool for forming people was a household catechism, written in 1529. Its three parts were the Ten Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. A father was to question his children and servants at least once a week. The young were to recite the parts daily and get neither food nor drink until they could. After each part came the question, what does this mean? At his table, Luther told his students that his wife, Katharina von Bora, had asked him why the old church prayed so hard, and their own household so coldly.

In 1530 the Emperor called a Diet to Augsburg, to deal with the Turk and to hear the quarrels over religion. Melanchthon wrote the Augsburg Confession for it. An elector, several princes and the senates of two cities signed it. Luther's name is not among them. The Confession rejected those who taught otherwise about the Supper.

In 1525 Luther wrote against the peasants' rising, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. The sources behind this account hold the 1525 writings, but not the 1543 treatise.

Luther died in the mid-1540s. In 1580 a fuller book of confessions was gathered, the Book of Concord. It drew together the catechisms and the confession given decades before.

legacy.text:
A confessional family grew from these churches. It still teaches a catechism like theirs, and it still sings in the language of the people, under many names. This account tells the churches as they lived in their own time. It makes no claim about what the later communities believe or practice now.

Three things are not carried forward. This account does not say what came after the church, run by princes and city councils, that these congregations lived under. It closes within a few years of Luther's death, though the confession it holds was gathered by 1580. The tradition went on for centuries beyond that point, in ways not told here. His 1543 treatise against the Jews is real and part of this history, but this account does not say how the churches that came after have answered for it.

docstory-witt.story.letter-to-albrecht-a.text:
On the last day of October, 1517, Martin Luther sat down to write to a man far above him. Luther was an Augustinian friar who taught theology at Wittenberg. Albrecht was Archbishop of Magdeburg and Mainz, and Primate of the Church.

Luther greeted the Archbishop as "Most Reverend Father in Christ and Most Illustrious Prince." He called himself "the dregs of humanity," amazed at his own boldness in writing.

Indulgences for the building of St. Peter's in Rome were being preached under Albrecht's name. Luther said he had not heard the preaching himself, and he grieved over what its hearers now believed. They thought a bought letter of indulgence made their salvation sure, and that souls flew out of purgatory as soon as a gift went into the money-box. "O God, most good!" he wrote. "Thus souls committed to your care, good Father, are taught to their death."

He asked the Archbishop to withdraw the instruction the preachers followed. Otherwise someone else might do it in public, to the Archbishop's own shame. He signed himself "Brother Martin Luther," and added one line more. If it pleased him, the Archbishop might look over "these my Disputations." They were ninety-five statements for university debate, sent along with the letter.

docstory-witt.story.augsburg-before-caje.text:
Years later, at his own table, Luther told his students how he was summoned to Augsburg in the summer of 1518. Frederick, the Elector of Saxony, gave him a strong escort and a safe-conduct, and he was warned not to trust the Italians.

He waited three days for the Emperor's own safe-conduct. In that time an Italian led him to Cardinal Cajetan, urging him the whole way to say one word, Revoco, which means I recant. Say it, the man promised, and the Cardinal would commend him to the Pope's favor, so that he could go home to his Elector in honor.

Before the Cardinal, Luther said, he knelt and then went all the way down to the ground. He stayed there until Cajetan told him three times to rise. The Cardinal was pleased, and he hoped, Luther said, that Luther would think better of things.

The next day Luther came again and would not recant anything. In Luther's memory, the Cardinal asked whether he thought the Pope cared for Germany, or that princes would raise armies to defend him. Where, Cajetan asked, would he be safe then?

"Under Heaven," Luther answered.

docstory-witt.story.worms-1521.text:
Years later, Luther told the students at his table how, at Erfurt, on the road to Worms, a herald asked whether he still meant to go on. Word had spread that he was condemned.

He had been summoned to the Diet under an imperial safe-conduct, he said, and the very next day it was broken. His books were burned at Worms before he arrived. He answered the herald that he would go, "although in Worms there were as many devils as there are tiles on the houses."

Before the Emperor and Electors, Dr. Eck asked whether the books on the table were his. He said they were his. Some were books of doctrine, and those he could not recant. He asked for time to consider, and was given one day and one night.

The next day the Bishops pressed him. God's Word, he told them, was not his word, so he did not know how to give it away. In whatever did not touch the Holy Scriptures, he would obey.

Word reached the Emperor, wrongly, that he had recanted. A Bishop came to ask if he had left his cause to the Emperor. He had not, Luther said, and never meant to.

docstory-witt.story.return-and-the-eight.text:
In March of 1522, Luther left the Wartburg, where he had been hidden since Worms. The Elector had told him to stay, but he came back to Wittenberg anyway.

While he was away, the reform had run ahead of him under his colleague Karlstadt and others. The town had fallen into disorder over how fast the old forms of worship should be swept away.

Luther preached eight days running. A witness named Kessler was there, and he said Luther first explained the day's Gospel. Then he "dropped the text and took up the present affair."

"And here, dear friends," Luther said, "have you not grievously failed? I see no signs of love among you." They had learned the doctrine, he told them plainly, without living it. "Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum."

The kingdom of God, he said, lies in deeds and works. "God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers," he said. They were to practice the faith that works by love, and a faith without love, he told them, was no faith at all. It was "a counterfeit of faith."

docstory-witt.story.brussels-martyrs.text:
Luther's ballad opens by calling itself "a new and wondrous story," sung "to his great praise and glory," the glory of God.

On the first of July, 1523, two young monks named John and Henry were burned at Brussels. Theologians from Louvain had examined them and pressed them to give up the evangelical teaching, but they refused. Word reached Wittenberg quickly, and within months Luther had written his song.

It calls them "two youths, highly gifted with rich and heavenly graces." In the song, the Louvain theologians try every device to make them recant, yet the two stand firm "like rocks." In its words, "for God's dear Word they shed their blood," and "they won the crown of martyrs."

The ballad says the monks' habits were stripped from them before the burning. They answered, it says, with "a cheerful Amen," glad to be free of "Satan's mock and masquerade."

docstory-witt.story.speratus-hymn-under-.text:
Wittenberg's first hymn-book was printed in 1524, and it held eight hymns. Four of them were Luther's own, and three were by Paul Speratus. One of those three was "Es ist das Heil uns kommen her."

Bacon, a later editor of Luther's hymns, notes a detail of the same book, the 1524 "Eight Songs." There, he says, Luther's three versions of Psalms are all set to this hymn's tune.

Bacon's Introduction also relates a tradition about the hymn. An unnamed wanderer came down from Prussia, the tradition says. He stood beneath Luther's window and sang Speratus's hymn, and the singing moved Luther deeply.

docstory-witt.story.first-german-mass-su.text:
Johann Walter, Luther's partner in music, set down in his old age, some forty years later, how Luther chose the Sixth Tone for the Gospel. "Our Lord Christ is a good Friend," Luther said, "and his words are full of love," and so he chose it.

Luther had written to the Elector of Saxony and to Duke Johannsen, Walter recalled, asking them to send Walter and the old musician Conrad Rupff to Wittenberg. They were to help decide how the church's tones should be set. Luther chose the Eighth Tone for the Epistle.

He set the notes himself over the Epistles, the Gospels and the Words of Institution, and then sang them over for Walter's judgment. Luther kept him at Wittenberg for three weeks, Walter wrote. Walter wrote out the notes for some of the Gospels and Epistles, and he stayed until the first German Mass was sung in the parish church.

Walter was to stay and hear it. Then he was to carry a copy of the Mass to the Elector at Torgau, from Doctor Luther.

docstory-witt.story.household-catechism-.text:
The two catechisms set out a program for every household, in detail. No source names a single household that kept it.

Mornings were to begin with the sign of the cross and a short prayer. It asked that "the evil enemy will not gain power over me." Afterward one might "go about your work and perhaps sing a song inspired by the Ten Commandments or your own thoughts." A father was to teach the Commandments in what the Small Catechism calls "the simple way," one at a time.

The Small Catechism also gave a servant words for confession. The servant was to say he had "served my master unfaithfully." The master or lady of the house was given words too, confessing they had "not faithfully led my children, servants or wife to God's glory."

The Large Catechism's preface made the weekly duty plain. A father was "to question and examine his children and servants at least once a week." The youngest were to learn the parts "word for word" and recite them each day. The preface says that "until they repeat them, they should be given neither food nor drink."

A head of the house was to hold his servants to the same standard. He was "not to keep them in his house if they do not know these things and are unwilling to learn them."

docstory-witt.story.diet-of-augsburg-153.text:
"Most Invincible Emperor, Caesar Augustus, Most Clement Lord." With that greeting opens the confession Melanchthon wrote for the Diet at Augsburg in 1530.

The Emperor had called the Diet to deal with "measures against the Turk," the ancient enemy of the Christian name. It was also to hear the quarrels over religion in the German lands.

At the close of the confession stands a list of names. It begins with John, Duke of Saxony and Elector, and goes on with George, Margrave of Brandenburg, and Ernest, Duke of Lueneburg. Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, is there, with John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, and Francis, Duke of Lueneburg. Wolfgang, Prince of Anhalt, is named next, and two city councils close the list, the Senate and Magistracy of Nuremberg and the Senate of Reutlingen. Luther's name is not among them.

Princes and city councils stand together and call themselves "Your Imperial Majesty's faithful subjects." They offer the Emperor a summary of their teaching, and they are ready, God willing, to say more from the Scriptures.

docstory-witt.story.household-and-kate-o.text:
His students wrote down what Luther said one day at table about patience. "I must have patience with the Pope," he told them. He went on to heretics and seducers, to the roaring courtiers, and to his own servants. "I must have patience with Kate my wife; to conclude, the patiences are so many, that my whole life is nothing but patience."

In another conversation, Luther told how his wife had been sick, and how he had prayed for her to recover. He believed God answered that prayer, and gave the household a good farm and a fruitful year besides.

At that time, Katharina herself is remembered asking him a question. She asked why, under the Pope, people prayed so often and so hard, while their own household was cold and careless in prayer.

Luther answered, as his students recorded it, that the devil drives his own servants on continually. They are diligent in their false worship, he said, while his own side is ice cold and negligent in prayer.

story.text:
From about 200 to 410 CE, Syriac-speaking Christians lived on the frontier between the Roman and Persian empires. Edessa lay under Roman rule, though its people spoke Aramaic, and Nisibis was a Roman fortress city from 298 until Rome gave it up to Persia in 363. Aphrahat wrote his letters from inside Persia. The city chronicle of Edessa holds the earliest trace of a church there. Written about 340 years later, it says a flood in about 201 destroyed a church building, though scholars dispute whether that line is original.

These Christians taught through song and symbol. Ephrem, a deacon, wrote teaching hymns called madrashe, and each had a refrain, so a congregation learned the faith by singing it. He read Scripture and the world through the raza, a symbol bound to the truth it shows. In this reading, Eden answers the cross, and the Jordan answers the font of baptism. In his Pearl hymns, he reads a whole theology out of one pearl, and the first hymn begins, "One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl."

These churches heard the Gospel as one continuous story. Around 172, a man named Tatian wove Matthew, Mark, Luke and John into a single harmony, which Aphrahat quotes and Ephrem explained in a commentary.

At the core of the vowed life of these churches stood the covenant, called the qyama. Its members were men and women who promised to stay unmarried for life and to serve the congregation, and they lived in town among their own families. The earliest dated witness is Aphrahat's sixth Demonstration, from 337, which speaks to an order already in place. Members were also called ihidaye, a word that means single ones and is also the Syriac title for Christ, the Only-Begotten. Later accounts say that women of the covenant sang Ephrem's hymns in choirs.

Who held authority was never settled in these years. Bishops led their churches, but the vowed men and women of the covenant had a standing of their own, and a trusted teacher also carried weight. Aphrahat drafted a letter for a meeting of bishops and clergy, though whether he was a bishop is unknown. In Persia, Papa, bishop of the royal city of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, claimed to lead all the bishops. According to later chronicles, other bishops fiercely contested his claim around 315.

Ephrem also defined the faith by answering rivals who preached in the same cities and the same language. Bardaisan was a thinker at the court of the king of Edessa, and his following lasted for two centuries after his death. Marcion rejected the Maker of the world, and his followers lived in the same region. Mani started a new religion in the third century. Ephrem answered all three by name, in prose and in hymns, and he treated them as one kind of deception, though their systems were different.

On the Persian side, faith meant endurance under a hostile crown. In the 340s, King Shapur II turned on his Christian subjects. Sozomen, a church historian of the 400s, says Shapur first taxed them heavily and then had their priests killed. Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, was accused of siding with Rome, and he refused to worship the sun and was executed with his clergy. Tradition dates his death to 341, though some scholars argue for about 344. Bishop after bishop was killed, and after Barba'shmin, a later bishop, was killed, the church's chief seat in Persia stayed empty for about twenty years. Roman Edessa was largely free of this persecution.

Around 400, Marutha, a bishop in Roman Mesopotamia, went to the Persian court as the Roman emperor's envoy. His access to King Yazdegerd I helped win royal permission for the synod of 410. That year the Persian state recognized the church, and the synod set it in order as one body, with provinces under Isaac, bishop of the royal city.

legacy.text: The woven Gospel of these churches did not last forever. Within a generation after 410, a new translation split the four Gospels apart again. Tradition credits Bishop Rabbula of Edessa with the change, but the sources leave open how much of it was really his doing. Once the harmony stopped being copied, its original Syriac text did not survive. It is known today only through fragments, quotations, and translations made from it in other languages.

docstory-syr.story.abgar-addai-legend.text:
This is the story the Syriac-speaking church of Edessa told of its own beginning.

King Abgar of Edessa was sick when his envoys came home from Jerusalem with news of what Jesus was doing. The king wrote Jesus a letter, saying that he had heard Jesus healed without medicines or herbs and opened the eyes of the blind by his word.

Abgar called Jesus either God come down from heaven or the Son of God, and he asked him to come and heal him. He had also heard that some were seeking Jesus' life, so he offered to share his own small and beautiful city with him.

Jesus answered, the story says, that the work he was sent for was now finished and he was going up to his Father. After that he would send one of his disciples to heal the king, and the city would be blessed.

After the ascension, Addai came. He was one of the seventy-two, and he stayed with a Jewish man named Tobias. The story says he healed the king and preached to the city, calling it away from Nebo, Bel and Taratha to the one true God.

In the story, Addai made Aggai leader in his place before he died. Years after Abgar died, one of his sons had Aggai's legs broken as he sat teaching in the church. Aggai died too quickly to ordain Palut, so Palut went to Antioch and was ordained by its bishop, Serapion. Serapion had himself been ordained by Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome, in the line of Simon Peter.

docstory-syr.story.edessa-flood-201.text:
In November of the year 513 of the Greeks, around the year 201, the river Daisan rose against Edessa in the night. King Abgar stood on the great tower and watched the water by torchlight. That same hour the waters broke down the western wall and swept through the city, overthrowing the king's palace.

The Chronicle of Edessa sets down this account. It was compiled about 340 years later from the archives where the royal scribes had filed it, and no bishop or believer is named in it.

One line among the losses matters most for the history of the church. "And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians." Whether the line is original, or was added later by another hand, is not settled. If it is original, a church building stood in Edessa to be destroyed, and that line is the earliest hard trace of a church there.

The entry goes on. "More than two thousand men were killed in that event. The waters came upon many of them suddenly as they slept in the night, and they drowned. The city was filled with the sound of mourning."

docstory-syr.story.jacob-nicaea.text:
Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, is remembered among the bishops at the great council of Nicaea. In the year 325, bishops from the whole world gathered there to answer Arius. The tradition of these churches holds Jacob to be one voice from their Syriac-speaking frontier, and says he stood with those who confessed the Son as true God.

Nothing survives of what Jacob said or did at the council. The lists of its signers were pieced together by later hands, and they carry his name among the assembled bishops. Theodoret of Cyrus, a Greek church historian of the next century, also counts him among them. Still, no document from the fourth century itself confirms that he was there.

At home in Nisibis, Ephrem praised Jacob as the city's wall.

docstory-syr.story.ephrem-roll-and-vine.text:
The Paradise is the Syriac version of a book by Palladius of Galatia. Its chapter on Ephrem opens with one dream and closes with another, though the Greek-based text of the same chapter has neither. The Syriac chapter does not name the first dreamer.

The Paradise says one of the holy fathers saw a dream in which the holy angels came down from heaven at God's command. One of them held a roll written on the inside and on the outside, and the angels asked each other who was fit to be trusted with it.

Some angels named one man, some another, and each time the answer was that these were holy and righteous, but not enough for this. They counted up many names of saints. At last they said that no one was fit for it except Ephrem, and they gave him the roll.

When the dreamer got up in the morning, he heard people saying that Ephrem was teaching. His words, they said, flowed from his mouth like water from a fountain. Then, it says, the old man knew within himself that the words coming from Ephrem's lips were of the Holy Spirit.

The second dream is one Ephrem himself is said to have had as a youth. In it, a vine grew out of his tongue and filled the whole space beneath the heavens, loaded with clusters of grapes. All the birds of heaven came and ate from it, and the whole time they ate, the clusters grew in number and in size.

docstory-syr.story.qyama-morning.text:
Before dawn in Nisibis, those bound by the covenant gather for the vigil. No single morning like this was written down, so this one is pieced together from separate sources, from the years before the city was handed to Persia in 363.

The covenanters are men and women who have taken the vow and stay unmarried. They walk through the dark streets from their own family houses, since there is no cloister. Among them, later accounts say, stands the choir of the daughters of the covenant, who will raise the madrasha, the teaching hymn.

The hymn carries the teaching on its tune, stanza answering refrain, until the whole gathering holds the argument by heart. The Gospel read out is the harmony, the Gospels woven into one unbroken story.

The feast this season keeps the Lord's birth and his baptism together in one observance, as Nisibis then did. When the light is full, the covenanters keep their fast and go back to their own households and their work in town.

docstory-syr.story.jacob-deliverance.text:
Ephrem's hymns sing that Nisibis was saved when Shapur, king of Persia, laid siege to it, but they say nothing of gnats. The story of Jacob's prayer comes from Theodoret of Cyrus, a Greek church historian, writing about a century later. Even the siege it belongs to is unsettled: it may be that of 338, 346 or 350.

Shapur's army lay against the walls, and the river had been turned against the city. In Theodoret's telling, Ephrem begged the aged bishop Jacob to go up on the wall and curse the enemy. The old man agreed and climbed into a tower, where he looked out over the numberless camp.

Then, Theodoret writes, "he called down no other curse on them than that mosquitoes and gnats should be sent against them." In his account, clouds of them came after the prayer and drove the elephants and the horses wild, until the Persians left their camp and fled.

docstory-syr.story.simeon-martyrdom.text:
"As time went on, the Christians grew in number. They began to form churches, and they appointed priests and deacons." So Sozomen, a Greek historian of the fifth century, opens his account of the persecution in Persia. The Magi, the priestly guardians of the Persian religion, grew deeply angry.

Simeon was bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, the royal cities of Persia, and he was accused of being a friend of the Roman emperor. King Shapur laid heavy taxes on the Christians, hoping poverty would force them to give up their faith. The year of what followed is disputed: 341, or about 344.

The tradition tells that Simeon was brought before the king in chains and would not bow down. He said he stood there now in defense of godliness and of the Christian faith. Shapur offered him gifts and then threatened to destroy him and all the Christians, but each time Simeon refused to worship the sun or betray his religion.

Usthazanes, the king's aged foster-father, rose to honor Simeon as he was led to prison. Usthazanes had been a Christian but had given way and worshipped the sun, and the bishop rebuked him and turned his face away. Usthazanes then confessed himself a Christian before the king, and Shapur had him beheaded.

The next day Simeon again refused to worship the king or the sun. That day a hundred other prisoners were put to death while he watched, and Simeon was killed last of all, with two aged priests of his own church.

docstory-syr.story.basil-legend.text:
Ephrem's fame reached the Greek church in his own century. Sozomen, a Greek historian of the next century, writes that Basil greatly admired him and was astonished at his learning. Basil later became bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Palladius of Galatia and Jerome both name Ephrem a deacon of the church at Edessa.

A later age built the story of a meeting on a passage in Basil's own writings. There Basil credits an explanation of Scripture to an unnamed Syrian, who, he says, knew little of worldly wisdom but much of the knowledge of the Truth.

Later tradition took that Syrian to be Ephrem. But Basil never names him, and he may well be another man, Eusebius of Emesa. The meeting itself is a later legend.

The later Life of Ephrem tells the story with love for both men. In it, a vision prompted the poet to travel to Caesarea to see the great Basil. The two holy men had no common language, yet they recognized each other in the Spirit. And Basil himself, the Life says, ordained Ephrem a deacon.

docstory-syr.story.choirs-tradition.text:
Later accounts say the daughters of the covenant sang the madrashe, the teaching hymns, in the churches.

How their choirs began is a story from the next age. Jacob of Serug told it in a verse homily around the year 500, more than a century after Ephrem died. Only that later memory says Ephrem himself founded and led the choirs.

In Jacob's telling, the people of Edessa were charmed by the songs of Bardaisan, a philosopher of Edessa's royal court, and by the songs of Mani, who founded a new religion. So Ephrem gathered the daughters of the covenant and taught them to sing true teaching in the same sweet forms. Through the women's voices, in this telling, his teaching reached the whole city, women and men alike.

docstory-syr.story.ephrem-famine-death.text:
In the last year of Ephrem's life, famine struck Edessa. Palladius of Galatia and Sozomen, a Greek historian, both tell of that year, writing a generation and more after his death. Their count of beds and the words they report come from remembered tradition.

For many years Ephrem had lived quietly in his cell, but now he left it and went to the rich of the city. He asked them why they had no pity on people dying around them, while their wealth spoiled into the condemnation of their own souls.

The rich answered that they had no one they could trust with the giving, because everyone was dishonest in such business. Ephrem asked what they thought of him, and they said they knew him to be a man of God. "Then trust me," he said. "See, on your behalf I appoint myself to take in and care for the needy."

He took their money and set up some three hundred beds in the public porches. There he nursed the starving and the sick, strangers and local people alike, and he buried those who died. When the year was over and good times returned, he went back to his cell. He died soon after, a month later in Palladius's account and a few days later in Sozomen's.

story.text:
The Reformed churches of two Swiss cities, Zurich and Geneva, grew up between 1519 and 1650. Huldrych Zwingli began Zurich's reform first, and John Calvin later shaped Geneva's, though the two men never met. Both cities held that a church has no standing to demand what Scripture does not support.

Zurich's reform began on 1 January 1519, when Zwingli preached straight through the Gospel of Matthew instead of the fixed list of readings. In 1522 some people broke the Lenten fast in public. Zwingli defended the act from Scripture, and the affair pushed the city toward open reform.

On 29 January 1523, six hundred people filled Zurich's Town Hall for a public Disputation. They came from across the territory, priests and laymen alike. Zwingli said that only Scripture could correct him. Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering as a "tinker's day." Their scorn moved a schoolmaster who had sat through the day, Erhart Hegenwald, to write an account. When the arguments were done, the council ruled for the reform and told every priest in its territory to preach the same way.

Within two years the reform split from inside. On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized Georg Blaurock at the house of Felix Manz, and Blaurock then baptized the others present. These were the first Swiss Brethren baptisms. Grebel and Manz had once stood with Zwingli. They argued that a church gathered only by a believer's own profession was the more consistent reading of Scripture. Zwingli's side held that the church should include the whole city, infants too. In the years that followed, Zurich's council moved to suppress the movement by civil force.

Zwingli left Zurich for the front on 11 October 1531, as a field chaplain in the Second War of Kappel, and he was killed that same afternoon. His close friend Oswald Myconius was in the city that day and later wrote down what he remembered. Myconius was not on the battlefield. He wrote that Zwingli was reported to have said, after he fell, "What harm is there in this? It is true, they can kill the body, but not the soul." Heinrich Bullinger succeeded Zwingli and led Zurich's pastorate for forty-four years.

Geneva's reform took another path. In 1536 the city broke from Savoy, and Calvin arrived. He was exiled to Strasbourg in 1538 and called back in 1541. Calvin built up the teaching article by article, in his Institutes and Catechism, and the Catechism was taught to all the people.

In 1541 Geneva's church laws set up a Consistory of pastors and lay elders. It could censure people, and it did not answer to the city council alone. Zurich's council ruled church and city as one, but Geneva's Consistory fought to stay free of that control. The Perrinist party opposed the Consistory, and by 1555 the fight was mostly settled in Calvin's favor.

Both cities refused two claims about the Lord's Supper. They rejected Rome's claim that the Mass repeats Christ's sacrifice, and they rejected Wittenberg's claim that his body sits in the bread. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529, Zwingli met Martin Luther, and the two sides could not agree. In 1549 people feared that Geneva and Zurich taught different things about the Supper, so Calvin went to Zurich himself with William Farel. What they worked out with Zurich's pastors became the Consensus Tigurinus.

Both cities held that God's free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved. They taught this as the ground of a settled life. Bullinger's Second Helvetic Confession of 1566 tells the anxious to look to Christ, the mirror in which they see their election. At the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619, Reformed churches from many lands pressed the same belief to its sharpest form yet. Their teaching passed on to the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism.

legacy.text:
The beliefs of these two cities passed on, unbroken, to four later traditions: the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed, and English Puritanism. No force from outside or inside ended the Reformed churches of Zurich and Geneva between 1519 and 1650. The end date, 1650, only marks where this account stops, for a tradition that is still alive. It is not a historical ending.

At the Synod of Dort in 1618 and 1619, Reformed delegates from many countries pressed these cities' teaching on election to its sharpest form yet. It came to Dort at one remove, carried forward from Geneva through the teaching of Theodore Beza. Dort sharpened a belief already held. It did not close or complete it. Dort falls thirty-two years before this account ends.

docstory-rzg.story.first-zurich-disputat.text:
Six hundred people met in Zurich's Town Hall on 29 January 1523. The city council had summoned the meeting itself. Priests and laymen came from across the canton, and delegates from the bishop of Constance came as well. They met to test Zwingli's case against Scripture.

Enemies of the new preaching, Hegenwald heard, mocked the gathering. They called it a "tinker's day," and said that nothing but tinkers were attending.

That mockery moved a Zurich schoolmaster named Erhart Hegenwald to write an account of the day. He had sat through the whole disputation. "I was there myself and sat with them," he wrote, "heard and understood and remembered all that was said there."

When the arguments were finished, the council ruled for the reform. It ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way.

docstory-rzg.story.myconius-account-of-z.text:
Oswald Myconius was in Zurich on 11 October 1531, the morning his close friend Zwingli left the city for the front. Myconius later wrote down what he remembered.

There were warnings that, looking back, seemed to have foretold it. The muster was disorganized: five thousand men had been summoned, and fewer than four thousand five hundred came. As Myconius watched Zwingli ride out in the rear, he felt a sudden pain of heart.

Zwingli was killed that same afternoon, and the news reached the city that night. The fight had been sharp, and it was lost.

Myconius was not on the battlefield, and he tells of the fighting as it was reported to him. Zwingli was said to have been struck down three times. Each time he rose, until a fourth blow brought him to his knees. On his knees, he was reported to have said, "What harm is there in this? It is true, they can kill the body, but not the soul."

The enemy found his body afterward. They tried and condemned it, and then they burned it. After they withdrew, friends of Zwingli went to look for any remains. Myconius was told, though he did not see it, that they found his heart whole and unharmed in the ashes.

docstory-rzg.story.calvins-journey-to-zu.text:
People who respected both churches, Zurich's and Geneva's, had begun to worry. By 1549 they feared that Calvin's teaching on the Supper differed from what Zurich taught. Calvin heard this often, and from worthy people. They wanted his writings to help them learn the doctrine of piety, and they did not want any sign of disagreement to hold them back.

Calvin thought a friendly conference was the best way to clear up the worry, so he went to Zurich himself. His colleague William Farel had suggested the visit, and Farel went with him. Calvin called Farel an "indefatigable soldier of Christ."

Calvin wrote that the two churches already agreed in judgment. The two men met with Zurich's pastors, and what they worked out together became the Consensus Tigurinus.

Calvin's letter afterward calls it a faithful record of the conference. It adds that every colleague serving Christ under Geneva's jurisdiction had signed it to show their approval.
